1ef30e7dace302aa: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 — The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) is demanding a comprehensive explanation from Meta regarding issues involving WhatsApp accounts that have been suspended, rendered inaccessible, or accessed without authorisation.
In a statement yesterday, MCMC informed that a total of 92 complaints related to the issue have been received by the commission so far.
According to the commission, an official request was submitted to Meta on September 25, followed by discussions with the technology company on September 28.

“Meta has requested until October 2 to provide feedback regarding the matter. MCMC urges Meta to provide a comprehensive explanation as well as an immediate solution for the affected user accounts, and will determine subsequent actions based on that feedback,” the statement read.

Earlier yesterday, Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said he had instructed MCMC to issue a statement clarifying Meta’s response regarding the issues of hacking and the deactivation of WhatsApp accounts.
He added that he has yet to receive updates on the outcome of the discussions between MCMC and Meta concerning the matter.

Earlier, MCMC announced that it was examining the complaints received and had forwarded the relevant cases to Meta for clarification and further action and the commission also explained that account takeovers or hacking, and account blocking, are two different matters.

According to MCMC, accounts hacked by irresponsible parties risk being misused for scam activities, spam, or violations of WhatsApp’s terms of service, which can ultimately lead to the accounts being blocked by the platform. — Bernama

6b50dc908bad6043: MANCHESTER: Abu Dhabi-based airline Etihad Airways said on Wednesday it was seeking legal advice on its options after criticising the Premier League's handling of an independent commission's findings against Manchester City.

The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million (US$1.2 billion) over nearly a decade.
Etihad, City's principal sponsor since 2009, said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication" that it was involved in improper commercial arrangements.

In a statement, the airline said the league never contacted or consulted it during the commission process and gave it no opportunity to provide information or challenge material that may have reflected adversely on the company.

"Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly," the statement said. "The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision."
City have denied any wrongdoing and said they intend to appeal.
A Premier League spokesperson said on Wednesday they would not be commenting on the Etihad statement.
Etihad added that the Premier League's public communication of the findings, following what it described as selective leaks and reporting, had harmed its reputation.
While reaffirming its support for Manchester City and its longstanding partnership with the club, the airline said it was seeking legal advice on the options available to protect its interests.
"We stand with the club, its supporters and our wider Etihad community as Manchester City challenges the commission's conclusions through the processes available to it," the statement said.--REUTERS
a43fe22734853ec6: JERUSALEM: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed Indian pilot Smit Machchhar for saving passengers after he was stabbed by his colleague in an alleged attempt to crash a flydubai plane on Wednesday.

Passengers on the flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday after customers and crew foiled the co-pilot's attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said. The struggle began when he stabbed the pilot and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.

Machchhar was covered with blood on the floor when he managed to click the release to open the cockpit door, a Netanyahu spokesperson told Reuters. That allowed passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot and enable a second pair of flydubai pilots who were on board to land the jet in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals," Netanyahu said in a post on X. "All passengers are out of harm's way," Netanyahu had earlier said in a video statement released by his office.

Indian authorities in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar is receiving necessary medical attention in a hospital in the northwestern city of Tabuk and they are in touch with his family and Saudi authorities to extend all possible help.
He is reported to be stable, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
Machchhar, who hails from India's financial capital Mumbai, underwent surgery after the incident, Indian newspaper the Hindustan Times reported.
According to his LinkedIn profile, Machchhar worked with India's SpiceJet airline for over 11 years before joining flydubai.

The cause of the altercation between the pilots was not clear. Flydubai said in a statement that the underlying reasons for the event remained unknown and warned against "premature speculation." It also suspended flights to and from Israel amid an investigation.

Netanyahu described the event as "a highly severe security incident", and said Saudi authorities would interrogate the co-pilot of flydubai FZ1073, which had been en route from the United Arab Emirates to Israel.--REUTERS
7e6be820e29b8955: KUALA LUMPUR: Integrity without compromise, fair enforcement, proactive prevention, greater use of technology and public trust will form the five pillars steering the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) as it approaches six decades in the fight against graft.

MACC chief commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman said the five pillars would guide the commission's administration and direction as corruption becomes increasingly complex and evolves alongside technology.
Speaking in an interview in conjunction with MACC's 59th anniversary recently, Halim said the commission could not afford to remain static.

He said the corruption landscape had changed significantly over the years, requiring MACC to continually transform and adapt its approach to remain relevant and capable of con-fronting emerging threats.

"Integrity is the main bulwark in the fight against corruption. It cannot be compromised for any reason, whether in making decisions, conducting investigations or carrying out daily responsibilities," he said.
Halim said this meant MACC would act against corruption regardless of the rank, position or background of those investigated, while demanding the same standards of integrity from its own officers.
"Integrity must become a culture, not merely a rule. It must be reflected in every action, decision and in the way we carry out the trust placed in us by the people."
FAIR AND EQUITABLE ENFORCE-MENT
On the second pillar, Halim said enforcement must be grounded in the law, evidence and principles of justice, and without fear, favour or influence from vested interests.

He cited MACC's decision to suspend the use of orange lock-up attire for persons under investigation during remand proceedings as an example of balancing firm enforcement with the rights and dignity of individuals who were yet to be found guilty in court.
"We can be firm against corruption while respecting the rights, dignity and principles of justice of every individual under investigation. That is the true meaning of fair and equitable enforcement."

Halim said the third pillar, pro-active prevention, reflected MACC's push to identify systemic weaknesses and close loopholes before they developed into more serious corruption and caused greater losses.

This includes strengthening public education and awareness, as well as examining practices, systems and procedures in public bodies to identify weaknesses that could be manipulated for corrupt purposes.
MACC, he said, was also increasingly adopting intelligence-based investigations instead of merely waiting for reports to be lodged.
"We want to act before the problem becomes bigger."
EXPANDING USE OF TECH
Technology and transparency form the fourth pillar, with MACC expanding the use of digital technology, data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) to strengthen its operational capabilities.
Halim said intelligence-based inves-tigations allowed MACC to identify indicators, patterns, connections and risks through information gathered from various sources.

The combination of data analytics, AI and digital systems could allow investigators to process large volumes of information faster, identify anomalies, trace financial flows and uncover connections that might be difficult to detect through conventional methods.

However, he stressed that technology remained a tool, with inves-tigators still responsible for evaluating, verifying and interpreting information and ensuring enforcement action remained within the law.
"We aim to build MACC's capabilities to be faster, more precise and always one step ahead in detecting and combating corruption, without neglecting transparency, account-ability and public trust."
Halim described public trust as the fifth and ultimately crucial pillar.
"Trust cannot be demanded. It has to be built through action, performance, integrity and consistency."

He said the strength of an institution should not be measured solely by the number of cases investigated or enforcement actions taken, but also by its ability to maintain integrity, professionalism and public confidence.
ENFORCEMENT PRIORITIES

Against this backdrop, Halim said MACC had identified four enforcement priorities for this year: government procurement, enforcement, public funds or special government allocations, and government revenue.
He said the four areas were selected because they involved substantial sums of money as well as powers and responsibilities entrusted to certain parties.
Any corruption, abuse of power or leakage in these areas, he said, would ultimately affect the public.

"In government procurement, for example, MACC has been looking across the entire process, from planning and specification-setting to invitations, evaluations, awards and contract implementation, as weaknesses at any stage could create opportunities for manipulation, conflicts of interest or leakages.
"The intensified approach has already resulted in significant enforcement activity this year," he said.
He explained that between January and Aug 31, MACC received 5,239 pieces of information, opened 842 investigation papers and made 803 arrests.
It also recorded 345 prosecutions and 97 convictions during the period.
"Of the 803 arrests, 311 involved civil servants.

"Based on the breakdown by offence, 352 arrests involved receiving bribes, 278 involved false claims, 78 involved giving bribes, 62 involved abuse of position, 12 involved money laundering and 21 involved other offences," he said.

He added that from January to July 31, MACC also recorded RM55.31 million in forfeitures, compounds and settlements, comprising RM12.28 million in forfeitures, RM42.24 million in compounds and RM786,556 in settlements.
BEYOND THE STATISTICS
However, Halim cautioned against judging MACC's performance solely by statistics.

He said the more important measure was whether enforcement could bring offenders before the courts, recover misappropriated funds, protect public money, address weaknesses and prevent entrusted powers from being abused.
"Numbers are not the only meas-ure of success," he said.

Looking towards MACC's diamond jubilee next year, Halim said the com-mission was also strengthening expertise in areas like data analytics, AI, digital forensics, digital assets, complex financial investigations and cross-border investigations.
"Internal processes would also be streamlined and digitalised where possible without weakening safe-guards and integrity.

"Corruption continues to evolve alongside borderless technology, increasingly involving complex and layered financial transactions across digital platforms, requiring MACC to similarly transform its structure, expertise and methods.
"We aim to build an organisation capable not only of dealing with pre-sent-day corruption but also threats that could emerge over the next 10 or 20 years.
"We cannot use yesterday's methods to deal with tomorrow's corruption crimes.
"MACC must continue to change, adapt and stay one step ahead," he said.

1a13f14bc6b31451: SIR John Templeton, one of the great pioneers of global value investing, famously observed: "Bull markets are born on pessimism, grown on scepticism, mature on optimism and die on euphoria."
It is one of the most insightful descriptions of how investor psychology influences stock-market cycles.
Templeton's message goes beyond market timing. It is fundamentally about understanding the relationship between price, sentiment and value.
The irony of investing is that investors often become most fearful precisely when prices may offer the greatest opportunities, and most confident when risks may be at their highest.
Born On Pessimism

Bull markets are usually born when investors are pessimistic. Economic conditions may be weak, corporate profits may have fallen, unemployment may be high and financial news may be dominated by bad headlines.
Investors become convinced that the future will remain bleak.

Consequently, share prices can fall well below what the underlying businesses may ultimately be worth. The market discounts not only today's problems but often assumes that those problems will persist indefinitely.
This is where the disciplined value investor looks for opportunities.
The key is not to buy simply because prices have fallen.

A falling share price can represent either an opportunity or a warning. The investor must determine whether the company's underlying economics remain sound, whether its balance sheet is capable of surviving the downturn and whether its long-term prospects remain intact.
The greatest opportunities often arise when pessimism causes investors to ignore the possibility of recovery.
Grown On Scepticism
As conditions begin to improve, pessimism does not immediately disappear. Instead, scepticism takes its place.
Investors may acknowledge that the situation is improving but remain doubtful about whether the recovery will last.
Earnings may begin recovering, businesses may report better results and economic indicators may improve, yet many investors remain unconvinced.
Ironically, this period can still provide attractive opportunities because prices may not yet fully reflect improving fundamentals.

The sceptical investor asks important questions: Is the recovery sustainable? Are earnings genuinely improving? Has the company's competitive position strengthened? Is management executing effectively? Are cash flows improving?
These questions are more useful than simply following market sentiment.
Matures On Optimism
Eventually, evidence of improvement becomes increasingly difficult to ignore. Corporate earnings strengthen, economic conditions improve and share prices rise.
Investors who previously doubted the recovery begin to participate. Analysts become more positive. Media coverage becomes increasingly favourable. More investors conclude that the worst is over.
Optimism replaces scepticism.
At this stage, the investment story becomes increasingly attractive to a wider audience. However, rising prices can create a dangerous psychological feedback loop.
Higher prices produce greater confidence, and greater confidence encourages investors to pay even higher prices.
The investor who bought when nobody wanted the shares is now sitting on substantial gains.
The question changes from "Is this business undervalued?" to "How much higher can it go?"
That change in thinking is important.
Dies On Euphoria
The final stage is euphoria. Investors no longer focus primarily on value and risk. They become fascinated by the possibility of extraordinary returns.
Valuations may reach levels that require exceptionally strong future growth to justify current prices.
Speculation becomes widespread. New investors enter because they fear missing out. People begin buying because prices have been rising rather than because they understand the underlying business.

At this point, rational analysis can be overwhelmed by emotion. The belief develops that the market will continue rising indefinitely. Traditional valuation measures are dismissed as outdated. Risk appears to have disappeared.
But risk has not disappeared. It has merely become less visible because optimism is masking it.
"The Time To Buy…"
Templeton's philosophy therefore contains an important investment lesson: the time to buy is often when others are reluctant to buy, provided the underlying fundamentals justify the investment.
This does not mean investors should automatically buy during every market crash or period of pessimism.
Some businesses deserve to decline because their competitive advantages have disappeared, their balance sheets are weak or their business models are structurally damaged.
The challenge is distinguishing between temporary problems and permanent impairment.
Likewise, investors should not automatically sell every stock simply because optimism is increasing. A high-quality business can continue creating value for many years.
The important question is whether the price being paid remains reasonable relative to the company's future cash flows and prospects.
Templeton's observation is therefore less a formula for predicting market tops and bottoms than a warning about human behaviour.

Investors should be particularly careful when their emotions are most comfortable. When everyone is pessimistic, courage and independent thinking are required. When everyone is optimistic, discipline and scepticism become increasingly important.
The cycle ultimately reflects a simple truth: markets are driven not only by business fundamentals but also by expectations about those fundamentals.
The intelligent investor therefore tries to think independently of the crowd. Buy when pessimism has created prices below reasonable value.
Remain sceptical when optimism is already embedded in prices. And when euphoria takes over, remember that an excellent business can still be a poor investment if purchased at an excessive price.
Templeton's enduring lesson is not to predict the market. It is to understand where emotion sits in the market cycle - and to ensure that our own emotions do not dictate our investment decisions.

eedd4c560b8a16ec: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's retirement age is back in focus as former Employees Provident Fund (EPF) chief executive officer Tan Sri Shahril Ridza Ridzuan calls for a review, while labour and employer groups differ over raising it.

Shahril, who is now Axiata Group Bhd chairman, said longer life expectancy and Malaysians' willingness to remain economically active could justify more flexible working arrangements beyond 60, including part-time work.

"This is something that really needs to be reviewed. The reality is that many Malaysians will continue working. When we reach 55 or 60, we still want to work," he told reporters after a panel session at the International Social Wellbeing Conference (ISWC) 2026 on Wednesday.
"So, in terms of the retirement age, perhaps we need to review it because life expectancy is also increasing. If we look at it now, it has reached 78 years," he added.
Shahril said flexible working arrangements could help older Malaysians remain economically active.
"Whether it is one or four (days) of part-time work, or perhaps through the economy, we should encourage people to remain productive.
"Because when it comes to retirement, if you retire but there is no productive use of your time, it is actually not good for you in terms of your mental and physical health," he said.
His call received support from the Malaysian Trades Union Congress (MTUC), which said it had proposed raising the retirement age for private-sector workers to 65 in 2018.

MTUC president Datuk Abdul Halim Mansor said the government had not agreed to the proposal at the time, citing concerns that a higher retirement age could reduce employment opportunities for younger workers.
"However, what we are seeing is that Malaysia continues to depend on foreign workers, with more than three million foreign workers currently in the country.

"MTUC's proposal is based on workers' capabilities, skills and good health. Raising the retirement age would help increase EPF savings and shorten the period of retirement to around 10 years, based on an average life expectancy of 75 years," he told Business Times.
He said workers who remained employed could also benefit from staying physically and mentally active.
Requiring workers to retire at 60 could leave them less active and affect their mental alertness, potentially contributing to earlier health issues and increased stress, he said.
"The retirement age should be formally amended under the Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012.

"Amending the minimum retirement age would allow workers to continue making compulsory contributions to the EPF under the Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, while ensuring that their employers' contributions and related benefits remain protected," Halim said.

He said workers would also continue to receive protection under the Employees' Social Security Act 1969, including employment injury protection, the Employment Insurance System and the 24-Hour Scheme.
They would also continue to enjoy employment benefits under the Employment Act 1955, including sick leave and medical benefits.
"These benefits would be available to workers through an amendment to raise the minimum retirement age to 65," he said.
Flexible Approach To Retirement

However, Malaysian Employers Federation (MEF) senior adviser for government, media and international engagement Datuk Syed Hussain Syed Husman said a blanket increase in the retirement age may not be the right approach.
The decision should ultimately be an individual choice.
"There are jobs where people are offered contracts after retirement and continue doing the same job. All of this depends on both parties and whether they want to continue.

"There are also opportunities for retirees to work on a consultancy basis, where they may only work a few days or when their expertise is needed. So, our employment environment is already quite flexible after the fixed retirement age of 60, or 65 in some sectors," he said.
Hussain, who is former MEF president, said the decision should ultimately be left to retirees, as they should be able to decide what works best for them.
"A one-size-fits-all approach to extending the retirement age may not work, as there are many other issues that need to be considered," he said.
Meanwhile, on lump-sum retirement withdrawals, Shahril said members should consider leaving their savings with EPF if they did not immediately need the money.
EPF could continue investing the savings and paying dividends, allowing members to plan phased withdrawals during retirement, he said.

"If you don't need it, or you don't have a better use for it, then just leave it with EPF. We will continue to invest it for you, you'll get a dividend, and you can then plan a phased drawdown. It's always better for you," he said.
Shahril acknowledged, however, that some retirees needed lump-sum withdrawals to meet financial commitments.
Those reaching 55 might need to settle housing or other loans, with their EPF savings potentially their only source of funds, he said.
Shahril said the broader challenge was ensuring Malaysians accumulated enough savings during their working years to meet their retirement needs and other financial commitments.
He said fewer members were making full lump-sum withdrawals at 55 compared with about 15 years ago.
"In the past, when I was first with EPF, 15 years ago, the percentage of people taking a full lump-sum withdrawal at 55 was very, very high. But now, that's coming down," he said.
Shahril attributed the decline partly to greater financial literacy and Malaysians accumulating more savings outside EPF.
He said Bank Negara data showed cash deposits and investments had also increased over time.

"So, I think people are generally better. And you would expect that because as a country matures and there's more income, people save more. But, of course, we still have to do the education, have to encourage people not to take everything out," he said.

202939bff0c99efd: MANCHESTER: Manchester City fans told AFP Wednesday they were "devastated" by the verdict on the football club's financial breaches, while supporters of rival clubs called for City's relegation from the Premier League.

An independent commission found the Abu Dhabi-backed club arranged "sham" contracts with a number of commercial partners to artificially inflate its revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million (US$1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
In that time, City won the Premier League title three times and also lifted one FA Cup and three League Cups.
Outside Manchester City's Etihad Stadium, retiree and City fan Mike Roberts said: "I'm absolutely devastated. I'm sad.
"I've been supporting this club for many, many years, since the 1956 FA Cup final. And I just don't know what's going to happen next."
Another supporter, Daniel Reed, a 41-year-old industrial designer, said bluntly the club had been "cheating."
But whatever the punishment, "the fans will always be there behind the team" and "take the brunt of it", Reed told AFP.
Former manager Pep Guardiola on X told fans "we will get through this together", backing the club's owners.
Sports minister Lisa Nandy warned Tuesday "the ultimate sanction is very serious indeed" and a club "can be expelled from the Premier League."

But Prime Minister Andy Burnham, former mayor of Greater Manchester, told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if the owners walked away, highlighting the investment the Abu Dhabi United Group had made in Manchester.
- 'WE ALL KNEW' -
Outside Manchester United's Old Trafford ground, fans of the rival team said they hoped City would be punished by relegation from the Premier League.
"We all knew they were cheating at the time," claimed Paul Griffin, a 57-year-old battery worker.
"The numbers didn't add up, you knew that what City were doing wasn't right, given the gates (ticket revenues) that they had.
"We lost those years – they gained those years. Stuff happens – that's football," he added wryly.
"I personally think it should be a relegation," said Corey, an 18-year-old student who supports Manchester United.
Connor Emery, a 25-year-old retail worker who supports Liverpool, agreed. "I would want a relegation, probably a points deduction to get them relegated," Emery said.
But he was sceptical this would happen, adding with a shrug: "It's probably going to be a fine, let's face it."
In initial reactions, former City defender Micah Richards told The Rest is Football podcast he was "absolutely devastated" by the revelations about the club where he started playing aged 14.

"I feel saddened. I feel angry. I feel a little bit confused," he added, citing a lack of information and conflicting accounts after the club's CEO Ferran Soriano slammed the verdict as a "Premier League conspiracy theory" and insisted the club would "be vindicated."
Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane said, if he were a City player, he would throw away all the medals.
"They knew it would hurt a lot of people, but they've still done it, and, if I was a player, I'd be 100 per cent sticking those medals in the bin," he told ITV television.--AFP

b1e44cc4f1eed57c: KUALA LUMPUR: Terdapat sebuah papan Scrabble terletak di atas meja di Merdeka Grill, dengan kepingan huruf disusun membentuk tiga perkataan yang kekal selama 71 tahun: I LOVE YOU.
Dr Mahathir Mohamad membongkok sedikit sambil melihat kepingan huruf itu. Di sekelilingnya ada hidangan makan malam, pastri, cahaya kota dan keluarga.
Ia adalah satu lakonan semula, tetapi bukan sekadar permainan keluarga biasa.
Adegan itu dirancang oleh cucu-cucunya untuk menghidupkan semula sesuatu yang pernah dilakukan datuk mereka untuk nenek mereka, Dr Hasmah Mohamad Ali, pada 1955.
Versi asalnya jauh lebih ringkas.
Menurut anak mereka, Mokhzani Mahathir, 23 April merupakan tarikh yang dianggap ibu bapanya sebagai permulaan kisah cinta mereka.
Tarikh itu begitu bermakna kepada mereka sehingga mereka terus meraikannya selama bertahun-tahun, malah kadangkala lebih mengutamakan tarikh itu berbanding ulang tahun perkahwinan mereka.
Namun, ada satu masalah pada 1955.
Mahathir terlalu pemalu untuk mengucapkan kata-kata itu. Jadi, dia mengejanya.

Perkara itu dikongsikan Mokhzani selepas Hasmah meninggal dunia pada usia 100 tahun, menambah satu sisi yang begitu intim kepada kisah cinta yang telah didengar rakyat Malaysia dalam pelbagai versi selama bertahun-tahun.
Pelajar perubatan muda yang suatu hari nanti akan berucap di hadapan parlimen dan presiden itu nampaknya tidak mampu meluahkan perasaannya kepada wanita yang dicintainya.
Scrabble memberinya cara lain.
Dia menyusun huruf-huruf itu dan membiarkan papan permainan tersebut menyampaikan mesejnya.
Ia kedengaran hampir ketinggalan zaman pada masa sekarang dan mungkin itulah yang menjadikannya begitu menarik.
Tujuh dekad kemudian, anak-anak Mokhzani memutuskan untuk menghidupkan semula detik itu untuk datuk dan nenek mereka di Merdeka Grill, Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur di dalam menara Merdeka 118.
Gambar-gambar itu merakamkan Mahathir di meja, dengan tangannya berdekatan kepingan huruf, sementara satu lagi gambar memperlihatkan mesej itu sepenuhnya: I LOVE YOU.
Tempatnya lebih mewah berbanding suasana asal, tetapi Mokhzani berkata perkara penting itu tetap sama.
Bapanya masih terlalu pemalu untuk mengucapkannya dengan suara.
“Mungkin sebab kami ada di situ,” katanya.
“Cara orang dulu-dulu.”

Perincian kecil itu begitu luar biasa untuk muncul selepas pemergian Hasmah kerana ia memperlihatkan sisi peribadi kepada sebuah hubungan yang kisahnya diketahui umum dan telah diceritakan berkali-kali.

Mereka bertemu pada 1947 ketika menjadi pelajar perubatan di King Edward VII College of Medicine di Singapura. Mahathir pernah mengingati bagaimana dia bersaing dengan lima lelaki muda lain untuk membantu membawa buku Hasmah. Apabila Hasmah kemudiannya menghadapi kesukaran dalam satu kertas peperiksaan, dia menawarkan untuk memberinya tuisyen secara percuma.
Akhirnya, dia turut memberitahu Hasmah bahawa dia mencintainya. Beberapa dekad kemudian, Hasmah mengenang bahawa itu merupakan perkara paling romantik yang pernah dilakukannya.
Mereka berkahwin pada 1956 dan menghabiskan 70 tahun berikutnya membina keluarga, meneruskan kerjaya dalam bidang perubatan serta mengharungi tuntutan kehidupan di mata umum.
Mereka juga pernah bertengkar. Hasmah pernah mengimbau bahawa selepas bergaduh, mereka hanya akan keluar makan.

ddf00b369396ed70: KUALA LUMPUR: Pertemuan khas bersama 25 Adun Negeri Sembilan malam tadi tidak membincangkan sesi menghadap Menteri Besar Ismail Lasim dengan Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.

Ketua Umno Negeri Sembilan, Jalaluddin Alias, berkata pertemuan itu sebaliknya lebih tertumpu kepada usaha memastikan semua wakil rakyat blok kerajaan terus komited melaksanakan amanah di kawasan masing-masing, selain memperkukuh parti.

“Kita bagi satu naratif, satu petua supaya Adun, 25 Adun yang ada ini menjalankan tugas di kawasan masing-masing, perkukuhkan parti dan juga tunaikan tanggungjawab sebagai wakil rakyat,” katanya kepada pemberita selepas pertemuan itu di Menara Dato’ Onn.

e52d9e06bba40113: MANCHESTER: Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell the club after they were found guilty of serious breaches of financial rules.
Burnham praised the ownership group led by Sheikh Mansour for its investment in Manchester since taking over the club in 2008.

"I would be really concerned to lose them," he told the BBC. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million (US$1.2 billion) over nearly a decade.
City have denied wrongdoing and said they will appeal.

Burnham, who was previously the mayor of Greater Manchester, drew parallels with Everton's battle with the league's profit and sustainability rules, when he argued the club he supports had not been treated fairly.
Everton received a 10-point deduction, that was later reduced to six points, after being found to have breached the league's financial rules over a three-year period ending in 2022.
"It would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before," he said.

With sanctions yet to be determined and appeals expected, Burnham acknowledged there was "a lot at stake" for City, their supporters and Manchester, but said it would be inappropriate for him to intervene in the disciplinary process.--REUTERS
8a43f4b054efdbb2: LES DIABLERETS: Switzerland's glaciers, which are disproportionately impacted by climate change, have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts said Thursday, with 2026 registering the second-biggest melt on record.

Swiss glaciers saw 5.5% of their volume melt away this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (Glamos) network found in a new study, published after a record hot summer preceded by a winter with little snowfall.
"The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice," said Glamos chief Matthias Huss, describing 2026 as "a catastrophic year".
Perched on the Scex Rouge glacier, at an altitude of nearly 3,000m, he gazed across the landscape in despair.
"This is a glacier that isn't surviving," he said.
"There will be probably no ice in 10 or maybe 15 years."
He carefully dismantled the four-metre-long aluminium measurement stake inserted at the centre of the glacier.
In late July, when it was installed, it was completely embedded, but now more than three metres protrude from the grey surface of the ice.
"It's not that we are surprised, because we know how fast the glaciers are melting," Huss said.
"But to see the colours of the mountains where there is no snow left, there is just these rocks and these dark glaciers that are a relic from the past... it's just incredible."

Between 2022 and 2026, the melt rate at Switzerland's glaciers was "more than twice as high as in any previously monitored five-year period", the Glamos report said, noting an ice volume loss of almost 20% since 2021.
While Switzerland's glaciers have long been shrinking, the melt has recently sped up dramatically.
While 10% of Swiss ice volume disappeared between 1990 and 2000, 27 % was lost in the past 10 years, the report showed.
Glamos based its findings on extensive measurements at 23 reference glaciers in September, which it extrapolated to the nearly 1,300 glacial formations still found in Switzerland.
'No chance of surviving'

The report comes after a summer where the months of June, July and August were each the hottest ever recorded in Switzerland since measurements began in 1864, according to the Swiss Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology.
This year, the protective snow cover on the glaciers had already partially disappeared during the June heatwaves, and had completely disappeared by September, even at high altitudes, Glamos said.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," Glamos said in a statement.

Due to significant melting this year, the researchers even had to reposition measurement stakes -- including on the highest-altitude glaciers -- further up after the ice melted away in the original locations.
The average ice thickness of some glaciers decreased by 2.5 to 4.0 metres, while the more exposed glacier tongues saw losses of up to 10m of thickness over the summer.
Rhone and Aletsch Glaciers
Although temperatures were higher this year, the ice loss did not surpass the record set in 2022, since many glaciers saw more snow before the summer melt than they had four years ago.
Less dust from the Sahara Desert also settled on the glaciers this year, allowing more sunlight to be reflected back into the atmosphere rather than being absorbed by the snow.
There were exceptions, however.
Four major glaciers experienced record melting this year, including the iconic Rhone Glacier and the Aletsch -- the biggest glacier in the Alps.
As the glaciers retreat, concern is meanwhile growing over the future availability of water resources.
Between July and September this year, the glaciers lost a total of around 2.2 trillion litres of water.
Huss said that quantity was "difficult to imagine".
"It's more than four times the annual freshwater consumption of Swiss households," he pointed out.
5df080da11c45397: KUALA LUMPUR: The battle lines for the Melaka election remain fluid as major political blocs struggle to seal electoral pacts, with analysts saying unresolved differences could result in multi-cornered contests if parties ultimately fail to reach agreements.

International Islamic University Malaysia political scientist Dr Syaza Shukri said the prospects of cooperation appeared to be diminishing, despite some of the larger parties having stronger incentives to seek electoral partners.
"It looks like the odds of them working with each other are falling. Interestingly, the larger parties appear to be the ones more keen on cooperation.
"I think this has to do with BN and PH wanting to retain, and be seen to retain, their hold on power," she told the New Straits Times.
Syaza said Pas appeared relatively comfortable with either cooperating with BN or contesting independently, while BN leaders in Melaka had from the outset appeared inclined towards going solo.
She said PH, meanwhile, may see value in working with Bersatu, but Bersatu could calculate that it had little to lose by contesting on its own.
Syaza said, however, a fragmented contest should not automatically be interpreted as an easy path to victory for BN.

"BN, specifically Umno, would have to compete against Pas and also Bersatu for the Malay votes," she said, adding that BN had won several seats in the 2021 Melaka election by majorities of fewer than 1,000 votes, meaning even relatively small shifts in support could prove significant.

Universiti Malaya political analyst Dr Tawfik Yaakub said the possibility of parties contesting separately had become more realistic, particularly as negotiations involving several blocs remained unresolved.
"If BN, PH, Bersatu and Pas eventually move separately, the Melaka election could become a highly fragmented multi-cornered contest.
"The key consequence would be vote splitting, particularly in marginal and mixed seats where relatively small shifts in support could determine the outcome," he said.
Tawfik said BN would enter the election with the advantages of incumbency, stronger machinery and a record in government to defend.
PN, meanwhile, could attract Malay protest votes, while PH remained relatively stronger in urban and mixed constituencies.

He said cooperation between BN and PN could reduce competition for Malay votes, while a PH-Bersatu arrangement could help PH broaden its Malay support base, although such a pact could create complications among sections of PH's traditional supporters.
Tawfik said Bersatu would also have to weigh the risks of contesting independently.
"For Bersatu, going solo would test its organisational strength and whether it can retain voters without relying on a broader coalition structure.
"The same applies to PH and BN, with each party having to demonstrate the strength of its machinery, candidate appeal and core support base," he added.
The uncertainty comes as all major parties have at various points floated the possibility of contesting the Melaka polls on their own, even as negotiations over possible cooperation continue.
Earlier, Bersatu secretary-general Datuk Seri Mohamed Azmin Ali said no agreement had been reached with PH.

Umno secretary-general Datuk Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki, meanwhile, said that BN could not force PH into an electoral partnership, but stressed that the coalition remained open to cooperation and was still in discussions with other parties.

4269b4551e7bacd4: PETALING JAYA: Analysts say Umno must demonstrate that its support for former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional pardon will not detract from its acceptance of the decision which saw him convicted in the SRC International case.
They said sympathy for the former Umno president should not overshadow the court’s decision or gloss over the weak checks and balances in place during the party’s time in government.
“Umno can support Najib’s pardon as a constitutional and humanitarian process, but it should not portray it as erasing or negating his conviction,” Universiti Malaya’s Tawfik Yaakub told FMT.
However, he said support for Najib as an individual must not be conflated with defending wrongdoings committed while in office.
Najib was jailed in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million in SRC funds.
He was sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined RM210 million.
In January 2024, former king Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah exercised his pardon powers by halving Najib’s jail term and reducing his fine to RM50 million.

Then, on Sept 18 this year, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of the fine and compliance with other stipulated conditions.
Umno subsequently set up a fund to help its former president to pay the fine, with party leaders, members and supporters encouraged to contribute voluntarily.
However, Tawfik said the issue ran much deeper, and that Umno must consider the wider impact of the case on the public and the country’s reputation.
He said the party must make clear that no public funds were being used, while ensuring that efforts to recover assets, pursue compensation and advance governance reforms continue.
“Umno does not automatically bear responsibility for an individual’s wrongdoing.

“However, as the party that led the government when the scandal erupted, Umno must acknowledge—in political and moral terms—that there were weaknesses in checks and balances at the time which cannot be repeated,” he said.

Tawfik said several reforms are urgently needed, including strengthening independent enforcement, ensuring transparency in political financing, mandating asset declarations, and tightening oversight of government-linked companies.
He said a clear separation between the interests of the party, the government and state institutions was also important to prevent such problems from recurring.
Meanwhile, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia’s Mazlan Ali said Umno’s “culture and governance” had changed little since Barisan Nasional’s defeat in the 14th general election.
“The party still follows its old ways,” he said.

However, Mazlan noted that Umno’s role in Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government had, to some extent, compelled the party to adapt to a political climate that places greater emphasis on transparency and integrity.
He said the Najib issue also highlighted differences in perception between some Umno supporters and other groups of voters.
Some rural Malays, Felda settlers, and Umno members and supporters viewed assistance for Najib as an act of solidarity and in humanitarian terms, said Mazlan.
In contrast, he said, many urban Malay, middle-class and non-Malay voters viewed Najib’s sentence as justified, given that the offences were established by the court.
Mazlan said that, to his knowledge, Khairy Jamaluddin was among the few prominent Umno figures to have openly acknowledged the wrongdoing and harm the case had caused the country.
However, he admitted that many Umno leaders continue to defend Najib, viewing him as a victim.
0bf83e4c1262a34f: PETALING JAYA: Umno perlu membezakan sokongan terhadap pengampunan bersyarat Najib Razak dengan sabitan mahkamah terhadap bekas perdana menteri itu, kata penganalisis.

Mereka berkata simpati terhadap bekas presiden Umno itu tidak seharusnya mengaburkan keputusan mahkamah atau persoalan tanggungjawab politik parti berkenaan terhadap kelemahan semak imbang ketika menerajui kerajaan.

Tawfik Yaakub dari Universiti Malaya berkata Umno berhak menyokong pengampunan Najib atas dasar perlembagaan dan kemanusiaan, tetapi sokongan itu tidak boleh digambarkan sebagai menafikan sabitan mahkamah.

“Umno boleh menyokong pengampunan Najib sebagai suatu proses perlembagaan dan kemanusiaan, tetapi tidak wajar menggambarkannya sebagai penghapusan atau penafian terhadap sabitan mahkamah,” katanya kepada FMT.
Menurutnya, sokongan terhadap Najib sebagai individu juga tidak sepatutnya berubah menjadi pembelaan terhadap salah guna kuasa atau penyelewengan.

Najib dipenjarakan sejak Ogos 2022 selepas Mahkamah Persekutuan mengekalkan sabitannya atas kesalahan salah guna kuasa, pecah amanah jenayah dan pengubahan wang haram membabitkan RM42 juta dana SRC International.

Pada 18 Sept, beliau diberikan pengampunan bersyarat yang membolehkannya menjalani baki hukuman secara tahanan rumah hingga 23 Ogos 2028, tertakluk kepada pembayaran denda RM50 juta dan syarat ditetapkan.
Umno kemudian mengumumkan penubuhan tabung bagi membantu bekas presidennya membayar denda berkenaan, dengan pemimpin, ahli dan penyokong parti digalak menyumbang secara sukarela.

Tawfik berkata persoalannya bukan sekadar sama ada sumbangan itu dibuat secara sukarela, sebaliknya Umno juga perlu menunjukkan keprihatinan terhadap kesan kes berkenaan kepada rakyat dan reputasi negara.
Katanya, parti itu perlu menjelaskan bahawa tiada dana awam digunakan, manakala usaha mendapatkan semula aset, tuntutan ganti rugi dan pembaharuan tadbir urus harus diteruskan.
“Pada peringkat parti, Umno tidak semestinya memikul kesalahan individu secara automatik.
“Namun sebagai parti menerajui kerajaan ketika skandal itu berlaku, Umno perlu membuat pengakuan politik dan moral bahawa kelemahan semak imbang ketika itu tidak boleh berulang,” katanya.

Tawfik berkata antara pembaharuan yang perlu diberi perhatian ialah penguatkuasaan bebas, ketelusan pembiayaan politik, pengisytiharan aset dan pengawasan lebih ketat terhadap syarikat berkaitan kerajaan.
Katanya, pemisahan yang jelas antara kepentingan parti, kerajaan dan institusi negara juga penting bagi mengelakkan masalah sama berulang.
Sementara itu, Mazlan Ali dari Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) berpandangan Umno tidak banyak berubah dari segi budaya dan urus tadbir sejak kekalahan Barisan Nasional (BN) pada PRU14.
“Budaya dan urus tadbir parti itu masih gaya lama,” katanya.

Bagaimanapun, Mazlan berkata kedudukan Umno dalam kerajaan perpaduan pimpinan Anwar Ibrahim sedikit sebanyak memaksa parti itu menyesuaikan diri dengan persekitaran politik yang lebih menekankan ketelusan dan integriti.
Beliau berkata isu Najib turut memperlihatkan perbezaan persepsi antara sebahagian penyokong Umno dengan kelompok pengundi lain.
Menurutnya, sebahagian orang Melayu luar bandar, peneroka Felda serta ahli dan penyokong Umno melihat bantuan kepada Najib, termasuk sumbangan solidariti, dari sudut kemanusiaan.
Sebaliknya, katanya, sebahagian pengundi Melayu bandar, kelas menengah dan bukan Melayu melihat hukuman terhadap Najib sebagai soal pertanggungjawaban terhadap kesalahan yang diputuskan mahkamah.
Mazlan berkata setakat pengetahuannya, Khairy Jamaluddin antara segelintir tokoh berprofil tinggi Umno yang secara terbuka mengakui kesalahan serta kesan buruk kes itu terhadap negara.
Namun beliau mendakwa kebanyakan pemimpin lain masih membela Najib dan melihatnya sebagai mangsa.
20e069c587b034e9: PETALING JAYA: Women are excellent at looking after other people.
You remember your children’s appointments, worry about your ageing parents’ diet and somehow keep everyone else’s lives moving along.
But when was the last time you asked yourself this question: “How is my own heart doing?”
Heart disease is sometimes thought of as more of a man’s health problem, but women need to pay attention too.
Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of death worldwide, and a woman’s risk increases as she approaches midlife.
Menopause changes more than your periods

During the phases of perimenopause and menopause, levels of the hormone oestrogen decline. Oestrogen has beneficial effects on a woman’s blood vessels and cholesterol, so as levels fall, her cardiovascular risk gradually increases.
Around this stage of life, she may also notice weight settling more easily around her waist, cholesterol creeping upwards, or increases in blood pressure and blood sugar.
Rather than fearing these changes, think of your 40s and 50s as a great opportunity to become more proactive about your heart.
Start by knowing the numbers. Have your blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar checked regularly and discuss the results with your doctor.
Eat to nourish your heart
You don’t need a special “heart-health diet”. What matters most is your overall pattern of eating.
Build meals around vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, nuts and seeds, together with fish, skinless chicken, tofu and other nutritious protein foods.

A simple way to put this into practice is to follow the health ministry’s “Suku-Suku Separuh” plate guide: fill a quarter of your plate with carbohydrates such as rice or other grains, a quarter with protein, and half with vegetables, adding fruit to complete your meal.

Fibre deserves special attention. Foods such as oats, barley, beans, dhal, chickpeas, vegetables and fruit help with cholesterol management while supporting better blood sugar control and digestive health.

Be mindful of foods high in saturated fat, salt and added sugar, such as processed meats, fried foods, pastries, biscuits, cakes and highly processed snacks. They don’t need to be completely forbidden. What matters is how often you eat them.
Snack smart too. Instead of automatically reaching for processed snacks, choose fresh fruit, a small handful of unsalted nuts, yoghurt, corn on the cob or steamed sweet potato.
Healthy eating isn’t about eating perfectly “clean”. It is about making nourishing choices more often while still enjoying your food.
Move your heart and strengthen your body
Regular movement helps your heart work more efficiently and supports healthier blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol levels.

Aim to gradually build towards a total of 150 minutes of moderate activity each week. That could mean 30 minutes of a brisk walk for five days, or you can divide it into shorter sessions that fit your schedule and fitness ability.
Even housework, gardening, taking the stairs, standing up regularly, walking while taking a phone call or a short stroll after meals are small pockets of movement that add up.

Include strength exercises at least twice a week using weights, resistance bands or your own body weight. This helps preserve muscle and bone strength, which become increasingly important during midlife.
Don’t underestimate sleep and stress
Women often wear exhaustion like a badge of honour. Please don’t.

Good sleep is an important part of cardiovascular health, while ongoing stress can make healthy eating, physical activity and blood pressure management more difficult. Making time to sleep, unwind or simply enjoy some quiet time is part of looking after yourself.
Put yourself back on your list
Taking care of yourself does not mean caring less for others.
As you move through perimenopause, menopause and beyond, let this be the stage of life when you pay closer attention to your own heart.
Eat well. Move your body. Build your strength. Know your numbers. Get enough rest.
You have spent years looking after the people you love. Your heart deserves some of that care too.

Indra Balaratnam is a consultant dietitian and a fellow of the Malaysian Dietitians’ Association. She runs her own private practice, Indra Balaratnam Nutrition, in Kuala Lumpur. Connect with her on Facebook and Instagram.
3f0bbca61c7fd594: KUALA LUMPUR: The special meeting with 25 Negeri Sembilan state assemblymen last night did not discuss Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir's audience with menteri besar Ismail Lasim, says state Umno chief Jalaluddin Alias.

He said the discussion focused on efforts to ensure that elected representatives from the government bloc remain committed to carrying out their responsibilities in their constituencies, as well as strengthening the party.
He said Barisan Nasional (BN) chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi urged the assemblymen not to be affected by current developments and to continue prioritising their service to the people.

"We conveyed a narrative and a guideline for the 25 assemblymen to carry out their duties in their constituencies, strengthen the party and fulfil their responsibilities as elected representatives," he told reporters after the meeting at Menara Dato Onn here.
He said the meeting was also attended by Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki and BN secretary-general Zambry Abd Kadir.
a0df7b68e0e314f4: LOS ANGELES: A popular California roller coaster is being permanently shut down after dozens of people claimed to have suffered brain damage while riding it.

The X2 at Six Flags Magic Mountain features precipitous drops and jarring twists that have thrilled millions of riders over two decades, with seats that swivel 360 degrees as cars travel at speeds of up to 80 miles (130km) an hour.
But it has also sparked a rash of legal complaints, including from two women whose families say they were seriously injured in July on the ride in Valencia, just north of Los Angeles.

Pamela Guillen, 40, suffered a severe subdural hematoma and brain compression after riding X2 on July 5, and underwent emergency surgery that required doctors to remove part of her skull, her family told CNN in an investigation last month.

Less than a week later, Naomi Greer-Wilkinson of Los Angeles, 25, lost consciousness after riding X2 and underwent emergency brain surgery, CNN reported. She remained in a coma for weeks and still can't speak or breathe on her own, according to her parents.
The ride has been closed since shortly after the second incident, but on Tuesday park managers said they were shuttering it for good.
"After almost 20 years, we have decided to permanently retire X2," park President Brian Oerding said.
"Since X2 opened in 2008, it has welcomed more than 16 million guests and earned a passionate following among ride enthusiasts," he said.

"While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it's the right thing to do. Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."
Attorneys at Dordick Law, who are acting for Greer-Wilkinson, said they had been contacted by more than 100 people who say they were injured by the roller coaster.
"The design of this ride makes it inherently dangerous, and makes it dangerous in a way that no reasonable rider would expect," attorney Christopher Bulone told reporters.
Theme park operator Six Flags, which has properties throughout North America, says it does not comment on pending litigation.
In August the company and ride manufacturer S&S Worldwide Inc reached a settlement with the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding X2 in 2022.
A separate lawsuit is scheduled for next year in which Sheila Katerelos, 56, alleges she suffered a traumatic brain injury on the ride in 2020.
2a7f68e93df4855c: NEW YORK: American Emma Navarro, a three-time WTA tournament champion, revealed a three-year battle with health issues on Wednesday, battling against her body as she found success on the court.
Navarro, ranked 24th in the world, said she will skip the remainder of the 2026 campaign to prepare herself for a 2027 Australia return.
"I'm taking the rest of this year to work on dialing in my medication and fueling protocols so that I can hopefully feel back to 100% again," Navarro wrote in an emotional Instagram post.
Navarro won the WTA Strasbourg title in May, was runner-up in June at Nottingham and reached her fourth Grand Slam quarter-final at this month's US Open.
But the 25-year-old said her dizziness and headaches from under-fueling her body only faded for her to feel comfortable a couple of months ago.
"I felt able to play tennis as myself again... to compete without it taking the life out of me," she wrote.

Navarro said she was diagnosed last year with RED-S (relative energy deficiency in sport), where the body does not receive the energy needed to support daily life and physical activity, and "Hashimoto's hypothyroidism".
After meeting with doctors and specialists last November, she was told she had been under-fueling for years and her body was fighting back.

"Over the past year I have gone all in," she said. "Although it took me a while to start feeling better, I gradually made progress. I began eating what my body needed to recover from the deficit I had been in.
"So yeah, I gained some weight this year, but I also gained my life back,
"I have enough energy to seize every day, to train and compete as hard as I want to and to live a life outside of tennis."
Navarro said in 2023 she began feeling frustrated and angry and became sick often.
"I couldn't think straight a lot of the time," she wrote. "I had trouble remembering things and articulating thoughts. My brain felt slow and tired, as did my body."
She reached as high as eighth in world rankings after a 2024 US Open semi-final run but became ill in China weeks later.
"I couldn't see the ball. I couldn't move. I couldn't play. I couldn't even feel," she wrote.
b5979525752bd901: TUMPAT: Residents of 12 small islands off the coast near here are worried after noticing speedboats in the area, believed to be operated by human traffickers.
The boats were suspected of ferrying undocumented migrants from a neighbouring country into Kelantan, often under the cover of darkness.
The residents said the boats posed a risk to fishermen and villagers who frequently commute between the islands, particularly those returning home from work at night.
They claimed that the boat operators were foreigners who were familiar with the landing points along the coast.
A resident in Teluk Renjuna, who wished to be known as "Pak Din", said villagers were aware of the boat movements but preferred not to confront the alleged traffickers.
"However, we are worried about accidentally crossing paths with them, especially because some of these groups are believed to have weapons.
"People here know about their activities, but we choose to keep quiet and hope the authorities will take action as soon as possible.
"We are worried when too many foreigners, including Rohingya, start landing near our homes because it can create problems," the 60-year-old former fisherman said.
The father of five said villagers were also concerned about the possibility of enforcement personnel colluding with the syndicates.
"The smugglers use speedboats at night without proper lighting. If they collide with a local boat, the consequences could be fatal.
"There was an incident where a smuggler's boat collided with a local boat. They paid compensation, but if someone loses their life, money cannot bring that person back," he said.
Another resident, who wished to be known as Ismail, said island residents could not avoid travelling at night as their working hours were unpredictable.
"People here do not have fixed working hours. Sometimes we finish work late and have to travel home at night.

"So, we are always worried about encountering these boats, especially around Teluk Renjuna, Pantai Haji Nik Mat and Pulau Suri. We are not looking for trouble with them. We are just afraid of an accident because their boats move very fast in the darkness," said the sundry shop owner.
The 37-year-old said residents had become increasingly cautious of the speedboats.
"If someone shines a light at them or accidentally exposes their activities, they may become angry. That is why people prefer to stay away," said Ismail.
Another resident, known as Wan, said the authorities should also investigate the presence of tonto or lookouts believed to be operating around the islands.
"The syndicates know every corner of this area. We hear there are more than 10 landing points to bring in migrants.
"They also have people acting as lookouts. These 'tonto' know the movements of the authorities and the routes in and out of the islands," said the 32-year-old odd-job worker.
The residents said the islands in the area were home to thousands of people whose livelihoods depend on the sea.
They said Teluk Renjuna alone had about 200 fishing families, while the wider island communities included boat operators and workers who frequently travel by boat.
They also claimed that many of the alleged human traffickers were believed to be Thai nationals.
The residents called on the authorities to increase patrols, particularly at night, and to identify the landing points and individuals assisting the syndicates.
The Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) acknowledged the potential risks to local boat users.
Kelantan MMEA director Captain Kamal Mohamad said his agency had increased patrols in the area, including from the estuary to inland areas.
He said the enhanced surveillance was aimed at detecting and preventing illegal activities, particularly the movement of undocumented migrants through the state's waters.

5fc2720e4f75437d: WASHINGTON: The US Justice Department asked a court Wednesday to punish federal judges in Minnesota who spoke to the media and criticised aggressive raids carried out in that state by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
It was the latest twist in a clash between the Trump administration and federal judges who have at times thwarted his drive to deport millions of immigrants lacking residency papers.

On September 17, The New York Times published an article that quoted Judge Patrick Schiltz, the chief judge at Minnesota's federal district court during a series of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids last winter in Minneapolis, and six of the judge's colleagues on the bench.

Schiltz had already gained notoriety during the peak of those raids by saying publicly that ICE had probably violated more court orders in January 2026 than other federal agencies had in their entire decades of existence.

In an interview for the Times article, Schiltz said ICE's behaviour had sparked such chaos in his court that it "created a grave threat to the rule of law." He said he thought the violations of court orders stemmed mainly from incompetence and staffing shortages.
It is rare for a judge to speak out publicly like that, the Times said.

He and the other six judges quoted in the article declined to talk about ongoing cases, but they did agree to address the tumult of last winter during the ICE operation dubbed "Metro Surge" and the tension it triggered between Schiltz's court and the Justice Department, the paper said.

The Justice Department announced Wednesday it had filed a judicial misconduct complaint against Schiltz and the other six judges at a federal appeals court. It accuses them of ethics violations by speaking publicly about cases pending in court.
The department asked an appeals court to investigate these judges, Attorney General Todd Blanche told a press conference.

The department has "asked that these judges recuse themselves from every case involving DHS, either criminal or civil in nature, because of the obvious bias they have shown in this article with the New York Times," Blanche said. DHS stands for Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE.

During operation "Metro Surge" ICE agents shot and killed two American citizens taking part in street protests against the immigration raids, triggering national outrage and prompting the administration to wind down the operation.
The administration says the raids netted the arrest of 4,000 people who were in the country illegally.--AFP

32aff4f1601343d5: WASHINGTON: Authorities in Pennsylvania confirmed Wednesday a fifth death linked to measles, as thousands of cases spread in the worst US outbreak in 35 years.
Lancaster County health officials confirmed an unvaccinated resident died of the highly contagious disease, without offering further details.
The region is known for its large Amish population, a traditionalist Christian community that avoids modern society and has lower vaccination rates than the general population.
The outbreak in Pennsylvania has affected 943 patients in 29 counties, state officials said.
Across the United States, as of Sept 24 there were 3,642 cases reported in 47 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Measles was declared eradicated in the US in 2000 after years of effective vaccination campaigns. The disease killed hundreds of children every year in the US before a vaccine was developed in the 1960s.

But the illness has made a worrying comeback in recent years as vaccine skepticism rose alongside growing mistrust of health authorities, spurred on by president Donald Trump's vitriol against public health leadership during the Covid-19 pandemic.

More recently, Trump's health secretary, Robert Kennedy Jr, has voiced vaccine skepticism, repeatedly spreading false information about the measles vaccine and downplaying the severity of the life-threatening disease.
Kennedy has also publicly questioned whether some recent deaths were actually caused by the illness, without providing evidence.
In Pennsylvania all the deaths have occurred in unvaccinated people.
Measles causes fever, respiratory symptoms, painful rashes and in severe cases complications can include pneumonia and brain inflammation, which can lead to death.
The disease continues to claim tens of thousands of lives around the world every year.
2566b84e06ef4220: LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday said there were "strong indications" Iran was involved in suspicious activity at a UK airbase that triggered a major security incident this weekend.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," Burnham told the BBC, referring to Sunday's bomb scare near the airbase in southwest England, which is used by the US military in its war against Iran.
"Of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation," said Burnham.

Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved in the incident, while foreign minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree".
Police said on Tuesday that no explosives were found at the scene. The nature of the threat has not been explained by officials.

Burnham's comments are the first official confirmation from UK authorities that Iran may have had a hand in the incident, which saw three white vans appearing to head towards RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday.
A local resident who rang the police said she saw a group of masked men near the vans, which were blocking a road in a village next to the military base.
The case was plunged into confusion when UK police released on bail five British men it had arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.
After three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said Tuesday they had found no explosives in the vehicles, but they had retrieved a "quantity of petrol".
Then on Wednesday, The Times newspaper reported that the incident had been foiled after one of the five suspects tipped off the police before the group was apprehended.

US President Donald Trump and his secretary of state Marco Rubio had previously indicated that intelligence bodies were aware of the suspects and that a foreign state could be involved, but UK officials had not weighed in.
"We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part," Burnham told Sky News.
Speculation was rife that Iran or another hostile state could have been involved, after Tehran previously warned London against allowing its military bases to be used by Washington.

Britain gave the US the greenlight to use RAF Fairford for defensive strikes against Iran, drawing Tehran's ire and unease from some residents in the Gloucestershire countryside where the base is located.

8ec7521382adac1e: KUALA LUMPUR: The Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Malaysia (Acccim) has cautioned that an excessive minimum wage adjustment could create a cost shock for businesses, particularly those operating on thin profit margins.
Its president, Datuk Ng Yih Pyng, said businesses had already been inundated with multiple cost increases over the past two years amid a challenging operating environment.
While not against an increase in the minimum wage, he cautioned that an overly large adjustment could impact micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Ng said the level should strike a balance between improving workers' incomes and ensuring the operational survival of MSMEs.
He noted that businesses with thin margins could pass higher labour costs on to consumers through higher retail prices, adding to inflationary pressures.

He said sectors with a large presence of low-wage and entry-level workers, including retail, restaurants, food services, agriculture and small and medium-sized manufacturing, would be particularly exposed to higher operating costs.
Ng also highlighted the "ripple effect" of a minimum wage increase, whereby workers earning slightly above the minimum threshold could also seek higher wages.
He said this could increase overall payroll costs as businesses adjusted wages across different levels to maintain existing wage differentials.
At the same time, higher minimum wages would directly increase employers' statutory contributions to the Employees Provident Fund, Social Security Organisation and Employment Insurance System.
Ng said a one-size-fits-all approach to minimum wage increases could put smaller businesses at risk of having to reduce their workforce or shut down.
Instead, wage increases should take into account productivity and performance, sector-specific financial capacity, as well as broader economic and business conditions, he said.

Acccim, he said, called on the government to consider a tiered regional system rather than a uniform national rate, taking into account differences in the cost of living, labour market conditions and levels of economic development across states.
He said a single wage floor could place disproportionate pressure on businesses in economically weaker regions, while workers in high-cost areas might still struggle to meet basic living expenses.

Under a tiered approach, minimum wages could be calibrated to local conditions, allowing higher wages in high-cost cities while helping low-margin businesses in weaker markets manage labour costs and reduce the risk of job losses.
