6e362be37deb0baf: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 — The East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) could begin carrying passengers as early as mid-December, ahead of its original January 2027 launch target.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said on September 23 that the government wants to see the ECRL completed before committing to other high-speed rail projects in the country.

Stretching 665km, the electrified rail network is set to transform travel between the East Coast and the Klang Valley, linking Kota Bharu in Kelantan to Port Klang in Selangor via Terengganu, Pahang and the Greater Klang Valley.
Here’s what we know so far about the ECRL and how close it is to opening:
1. How fast is the ECRL, and where will it run?

The ECRL network is being developed in two phases: the Kota Bharu-to-Gombak stretch, originally slated to begin operations in January 2027, and the Gombak-to-Port Klang section, scheduled to open in January 2028.

Transport Minister Anthony Loke said in August that the first phase was on track for completion in December, with the government pushing for passenger operations to begin as early as the middle of that month.
The passenger fleet will comprise 11 six-car Electric Multiple Unit (EMU) train sets built by China Railway Rolling Stock Corporation (CRRC) Dalian.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Transport Minister Anthony Loke challenged MRL and CCCC in August 2026 to bring forward the start of ECRL operations to mid-December. — Picture by Raymond Manuel

Malaysia Rail Link Sdn Bhd (MRL) chief executive officer Datuk Seri Darwis Abdul Razak told Bernama in September that the ECRL would nearly halve the travel time between Kota Bharu and Gombak, from about seven hours by road to around four hours.
ECRL services could also run from Gombak to Kuala Terengganu in about three hours and from Gombak to Kuantan in just one hour and 35 minutes on an express service, according to Loke.
The full ECRL network is planned to have 20 stations, comprising 10 passenger-only stations and 10 stations serving both passengers and freight.
2. How many passengers can the ECRL carry?
Each six-car EMU can carry up to 425 passengers in an all-economy configuration.

The passenger trains will operate at speeds of up to 160km/h and are equipped with facilities including toilets, luggage racks, food-and-beverage counters, prayer rooms with ablution areas and facilities for passengers with disabilities.
Loke has said the network could eventually carry up to 10,000 passengers a day, depending on service frequency.
3. Why is the ECRL being pushed for an earlier opening?
Loke recently challenged MRL and China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) to get the first phase of the ECRL running in time for the year-end school holidays in mid-December.
The earlier launch, however, remains subject to testing and commissioning being completed satisfactorily and without compromising safety requirements.

CCCC is the ECRL’s engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning contractor, while operations and maintenance will be handled through a joint venture involving MRL and China Communications Construction Company ECRL Sdn Bhd (CCCECRL).
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A general view of the ECRL tunnel in Section 2A in Rawang during a technical site visit on October 31, 2025. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
4. How close is the ECRL to opening?
MRL is already deploying comprehensive inspection trains (CITs) to detect potential problems along the rail network ahead of the planned start of operations.
More than 40 CIT test runs and 12 freight train tests had been carried out as of September 18, CCCECRL project director and senior adviser Kong Qi told The Edge Malaysia recently.
The testing has included speeds of up to 176km/h, above the ECRL’s planned passenger operating speed of 160km/h.
The trains are expected to complete full runs between Kota Bharu and Gombak by the end of September, before the mandatory Fault-Free Run (FFR) begins in October.
The Transport Ministry is also expected to announce ECRL fares by the end of the year.
5. Will the ECRL carry freight too?
Yes. The ECRL will also deploy electric locomotives for freight services along the network.
The freight trains can operate at speeds of up to 80km/h and haul as many as 45 wagons, with a maximum freight capacity of 3,500 tonnes per trip, the New Straits Times reported last December.
The electric locomotives are also equipped with intelligent human-machine interfaces and millisecond-level safety monitoring systems covering braking, fire protection and high-voltage insulation.
0ce30a0e61f4ea75: KETAPANG (Indonesia), Oct 1 — Housework in the morning followed by several hours of firefighting: women in Indonesian Borneo risk life and limb to battle blazes making their communities sick, all while shouldering a sexist backlash.
More than 100 women, many of them homemakers, are volunteer members of an initiative dubbed “Power of Mama”, patrolling daily for smoke and flames and jumping in to put out fires when needed.
Formed in 2022, the “Mamas”, as they call themselves, are spread over a dozen villages in the Ketapang regency of rural Kalimantan — the name for Indonesia’s part of Borneo.
It is a region where traditional gender roles define women as the main providers of childcare, cooking and cleaning, and where firefighting is a male domain.
“There have been sarcastic remarks,” homemaker and mother Ramilah, 46, told AFP in Tanjungpura village after helping battle a nearby peatland fire with more than a dozen other women.
“We have explained that our intention is good, to help... and Alhamdulillah (praise be to God), the community has begun to accept it,” said Ramilah, who, like many Indonesians, has only one name.
The women set out on a smoke-saturated September Saturday — some on motorbikes, others piled onto the back of a pickup truck with a water pump and some buckets.
They wore orange jump suits and rubber boots for protection, most sporting hijabs under their hard hats.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The women setting out, some on motorbikes, others piled onto the back of a pickup truck with a water pump and some buckets. — AFP pic
Surgical masks were their only shield against the toxic smoke in which they battled for hours.
Peatland fires are common in Kalimantan and can smoulder and spread under the soil for weeks or months, emitting huge quantities of smoke and sometimes causing surface blazes.
‘Protect our forest’
Ramilah said she joined the initiative “to protect our forest” and counter the toxic haze emitted by the fires that has “had a big impact — especially for my child, who now can’t go to school”.
It makes for much longer days.
Ramilah starts at the crack of dawn with housework, taking care of the cows and feeding the family’s stock of tilapia fish.
Fire patrols and operations are from about 10am to 1pm, “then working at home again until night”, she said.

The “Power of Mama”, with backing from Indonesia’s YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation, was inspired by the hardships experienced in 2019, when wildfires ravaged Kalimantan during another tough episode of the El Nino weather phenomenon that typically brings severe drought to Indonesia.
Wildfires in Indonesia are blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that result in the destruction of fire-resistant forest cover and the draining of peatlands.
Nearly 900,000 hectares (3,475 square miles) of land have burnt in Indonesia so far this year, according to the Nusantara Atlas fire monitor — more than five times the size of Greater London.
Government figures put the razed area at just over 202,000 hectares between January and July.
The resulting haze has spread to neighbouring countries, closed thousands of schools, caused tens of thousands of respiratory infections and imperilled countless wild animals.
‘Women are not suited’
“Power of Mama” coordinator Mita Anggraeni told AFP sexism had been a challenge.
“Some people still think that women are not suited... to handle fires” despite often being at the forefront when they strike.
“When the men work far away, the women who stay in the village have to go out themselves to put out the fire,” Mita said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The ‘Mamas’ on a break during a patrol mission in the Benipis area, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan on September 27, 2026. — AFP pic
Melyanti, a 25-year-old carer for the elderly and part-time firefighter, told AFP there were some in the community “who don’t like our fire prevention activities”.
“If anyone asks for help, as long as our group is able to help, we will,” she said.
But when the land of a vocal detractor recently caught fire, “we didn’t respond. We couldn’t help because he had belittled us for two months”.
Homemaker and mother Mutia Mulansari, 30, said she had heard people say the women were “just riding motorbikes back and forth, back and forth... we’re just playing around”.
But attitudes have begun changing as the volunteers “proved that we are capable”, she said.
Her husband Roni Irawan, 35, said he supported Mutia’s firefighting endeavours, especially since she showed she was “still able to manage the housework”.
“It turns out that mothers can do more than work in the home,” Mutia said. — AFP
c5994e12072465a2: RIVNE (Ukraine), Oct 1 — Illegal amber mining has blighted the landscape in Rivne, northwest Ukraine, leaving just tree stumps, small bushes and swampy puddles deep in the coniferous forest.
Mafia-style groups flushed out chunks of the golden fossilised resin for years, paying little regard to the environment, fuelling a black market industry that devastated thousands of hectares.
Amber is used to make jewellery and other products, which are hugely sought after in China.
Ukraine started regulating the industry just a few years before Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
But stretched for resources during a war that has become the biggest in Europe since World War II, industry figures now warn that fragile progress in cleaning up the lucrative sector is being wasted.

Unregistered — so-called “grey” — amber is flooding the market, environmental inspections have been suspended and firms are relying on private security groups, armed with weapons siphoned from the front, to protect their sites.

“There are many dishonest operators, a very, very large percentage of dishonest subsoil users,” Oleg Bogelsky, co-owner of Ukraine’s Amber Galbin group, a mining company with operations in Rivne, told AFP.
He estimated about 60 to 70 per cent of all amber being mined in Ukraine is “grey”.
‘Real chaos’
Ukraine has some of the world’s biggest reserves of amber, the deep golden resin known as the “sun stone”.
After the Soviet Union collapsed in the 1990s, rogue operators swooped to cash in on surging Chinese demand.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Employees process amber at a production facility of the Amber Galbin group in Rivne. — AFP pic
Large-scale miners controlled by criminal groups devastated the countryside as they flushed out huge quantities of amber using motor pumps, becoming known as the “amber mafia”.
There was little in the way of legislation, regulation or enforcement to stop them.
It was “real chaos” that led to an ecological “catastrophe”, said Olena Belichenko, an expert at the International Amber Association.
“Mining was carried out illegally, the environment was effectively suffering, and our resources were being plundered for 30 years,” said Bogelsky.
2,000 illegal miners
Andriy Lototsky, director of the Sonyachne Remeslo mining company, is matter-of-fact about how he got involved in the industry.
“Like everyone else, illegally,” he told AFP.
“No one paid attention to plants or trees. Everything in their path was just knocked down.”
Ivan Shvyryd of Volodymyrets Forestry, a government forest protection agency, recalled turning up at one illegal extraction site with a handful of police, to find “2,000 people digging”.
“When a fifth-grade child doesn’t go to school and goes to dig for amber instead... isn’t that a shame?”
Ukraine in 2019 passed a long-awaited law regulating amber mining, mandating less intrusive practices and excavator-digging based on approved plans.
Permits were issued mainly for areas heavily damaged by the illegal mining, with private businesses then forced to put the land back into proper condition.
Official amber extraction and exports steadily grew.
On-the-book exports of unprocessed amber rose from 0.61 tonnes in 2020 to 88.83 tonnes in 2025, according to data from Ukraine’s Customs Service obtained by AFP.
But martial law, imposed in 2022 when Russia invaded, suspended scheduled inspections and environmental audits, leaving regulators little insight into what is happening on the ground.
“Some subsoil users abuse their position and, perhaps, some extract illegally,” Mykola Kotniuk, chairman of the Amber Business Association of Ukraine, conceded.
He said groups that only have permits for pilot and exploratory work may be extracting.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Workers extract amber at the official open cast mine in the Rivne region. — AFP pic
Competitive edge
Cases of flagrantly illegal pumping are still “isolated”, said Lototsky.
Ukraine has opened 369 probes into illicit amber mining and possession since 2024, the head of the Specialised Environmental Prosecutor’s Office Borys Indychenko told AFP.
They include a mining ring uncovered in June 2026, led by a local official, accused of causing some $8 million in environmental damage.

According to a report by Intelligence Online, companies are bringing in private security contractors armed with black market weapons stolen from the front line to protect their sites from being ransacked.
“Enterprises set up fences and checkpoints, and in some cases, bring in security guards who may be part of an organised criminal group,” prosecutor Indychenko said.
Legitimate players are calling on the state to resume inspections and put the industry on a tighter leash — saying those who bend the rules are at a competitive advantage.

“If we now sit down together with honest subsoil users and the state and adjust the vectors a bit, change direction a little... then of course we will become number one in the world,” said Bogelsky. — AFP
c1fb04d56fae7cb5: THYMAINA (Greece), Oct 1 — “Let’s go to war!” shouted six-year-old Giorgos at his older cousin, Minas, as the two chased each other with claw-like geranium stalks around the schoolyard on the tiny Greek island of Thymaina.
The two boys are the last primary school children on the far-flung eastern Aegean island, 40 kilometres (25 miles) from the Turkish coast.
“When I was a boy, the school had nearly 70 children,” 77-year-old Manolis Mitikas, owner of Thymaina’s portside cantina, mused over a game of backgammon.
Like the rest of Greece, the former pirate hideout is facing the effects of an ageing population.
The education ministry said it was shuttering 43 nurseries and 32 primary schools this year “due to very low to non-existent” student numbers.
Another 70 nurseries were merged.
The challenge is even greater in small Aegean islands far from the Greek mainland.

“If we have no more children, the school will close... and unfortunately, we have no more children in Thymaina,” Marigo Kottara, deputy mayor of the Fournoi archipelago of which the island is part, told AFP.
Greece last year recorded fewer than 66,000 births compared to more than 107,000 in 2005, with the population estimated to fall by more than a million to 9.2 million by 2050.
Thymaina no longer has a nursery, and its high school closed years ago.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph shows a view of the Aegean Sea from the island of Thymaina on September 23, 2026.
Six teenagers still living on the island take a boat to neighbouring Fournoi every morning.
Thymaina’s sole teacher, Konstantinos Fantelas, has to teach the boys everything from Greek to maths, history, religion and music.

Thymaina is only served by two ferries a week linking it to the capital Athens — a journey that takes at least eight hours, with a final hop from Fournoi. The connection can frequently be disrupted by poor weather, leaving islanders stranded for days.
Pirate lore
Fournoi’s cluster of islands off Samos have many secluded coves that for centuries were perfect for piracy.
The Mitikas family claims descent from the area’s last known pirate, Emmanouil Mitikas, who was executed in the 1860s.
“The pirate Mitikas was my father-in-law’s grandfather,” said Maria Markaki, a restaurant owner in Fournoi.
“My husband is still a pirate, he can’t get enough of the sea,” she joked.
The waters around the island have over 60 known shipwrecks dating back to the 6th century BCE.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A local walks along the port on the Aegean island of Thymaina.
Municipal officials now hope that a decade-long culture ministry initiative to open underwater archaeology parks in the area will draw more visitors.
The first of three is to open next year, Kottara said.
Cash incentives
Greece’s downsizing of schools has drawn complaints from neighbouring Turkey, which criticised Athens in July for closing down eight schools catering to the country’s Turkish-speaking minority.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has described Greece’s demographic problem as a “national danger”.
His government — which faces elections next year — this month promised tax breaks to parents with three children, and extra cash for parents who have more than three.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Minas and Giorgos, the only two primary school students on Thymaina. — AFP pic
But with many Greek families making do with salaries of under 1,000 euros (RM4,600) amid skyrocketing energy prices, some local officials are taking matters into their own hands.
Earlier this month Nisyros, a small Dodecanese island with a population of just over 1,000, said it would offer 3,000 euros for each child born to permanent residents.
“It is the message that Nisyros believes in its future, and that future is our children,” island mayor Christofis Koronaios said.
In Thymaina locals have waited for years for works to improve the island’s harbour and dirt road network.
“What are we supposed to do, raise the Turkish flag?” asked one angry islander. — AFP
eb73c461a18d53a7: SYDNEY, Oct 1 — After trawling through dozens of applications, the hunt is over: an Australian animal welfare group has found a successor to a hero hound credited with saving more than 100 koalas from fires.
Bear surrendered his collar in March after a decade of being a very good boy as one of the first dogs in the country to be trained to detect the scent of koala fur.
Those skills were critical in helping rescuers to find marsupial survivors of bush fires.
With Bear’s retirement, the International Fund for Animal Welfare launched a search for his successor, admitting: “He’s leaving very big boots to fill.”
Among dozens of applications from across the country—and as far afield as the United States—an Australian koolie called Oaka stood out.
“We didn’t know it would be possible to find a new Bear. He was truly one of a kind... but then along came Oaka,” said Josey Sharrad, the welfare fund’s Oceania head of programmes.
“Bear showed the world what’s possible when a rescue dog is given a second chance and finds its true purpose. I see that same spark in Oaka.”
Oaka, like Bear, was considered “too much to handle” by her family, the group said.
But her potential was spotted by a local rescue group, who submitted an application. She then passed the initial test “with flying colours”.
The animal welfare group’s director of canine units, Frederic Chappee said Oaka was “almost too good to be true”.

“For many people around the world, Bear became an icon. But what makes Bear truly unique is not only what he achieved, but the void he left behind. It’s a void that I am hopeful Oaka can fill,” he said.

Bear’s skills saved over 100 koalas as the Black Summer bushfires raged across Australia’s eastern seaboard from late 2019 to early 2020, razing millions of hectares, destroying thousands of homes and blanketing cities in noxious smoke.
With Australia’s fire services warning that the start of the northern hemisphere summer later this year could see more intense blazes, Oaka’s training will be fast-tracked.
“We know how critical it is to have a highly skilled koala detection dog back in the field, helping protect one of Australia’s most iconic species,” Sharrad said.
“With El Nino already here and a tough summer on the horizon, our koalas will need all the help they can get, whether it comes on two legs or four.” — AFP
e599a9994864d845: KOTA BHARU, Oct 1 — As the lights dim, the white screen becomes the centre of attention, its surface slowly coming alive with shadows.

Behind it, the tok dalang (puppeteer) moves the intricately carved puppets with remarkable precision, making them glide, bow, fight or dance as their silhouettes unfold against the screen, known as kelir in Javanese.
The rhythmic beat of the traditional Malay orchestra rises and falls with the unfolding story, punctuated by the voices of the tok dalang and the occasional laughter of the audience.
To the audience, the colourful puppets remain hidden from view; only their sharply defined shadows appear to bring stories such as ‘Hikayat Seri Rama’ or local tales to life.
The puppets used in wayang kulit performances are no mere “toys” - each of them is meticulously crafted and detailed by artisans who are often tok dalang themselves.

“The main characters (puppets) feature intricate floral motifs and delicate patterns, but of course audiences cannot see them. Making each puppet is not only time-consuming but also painstaking. As the Kelantanese would say, ‘boleh keluar putih mata’, because the work is intricate and requires intense concentration,” said Kelantan wayang kulit practitioner Kang Boon Ann, better known as Che Ann.

Che Ann, a Peranakan Chinese, is among the few people in Kelantan who remain actively involved in preserving wayang kulit, a traditional shadow puppet theatre more closely associated with the Malay community.
His wife and two children are also involved in staging wayang kulit performances, under the banner of the Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association.
**NP_IMAGE_BODY[365469]**<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

In a *wayang kulit* (shadow puppetry) performance, what the audience sees on the white screen are merely the silhouettes of puppets; these are manipulated by the *tok dalang* (master puppeteer) to enact tales such as the *Hikayat Seri Rama* in the Kelantan style, or local stories in the *wayang kulit Gedek* tradition. However, behind those black shadows lie colorful puppets, each meticulously carved and shaped by an artisan—who is typically the *tok dalang* himself. — Bernama pic
Handmade

Falling in love with wayang kulit puppets at the age of seven, Che Ann, 58, has devoted more than three decades to making the puppets while also serving as tok dalang of the Sri Cindayu Wayang Kulit Association.
Speaking to Bernama at his workshop in Kok Lanas here, Che Ann described the puppets as the “soul” of every wayang kulit performance.
On how the puppets are made, he said they are made from cowhide, which must undergo several processes before it can be used.

“We use cowhide because it is soft and its natural characteristics make it most suitable for making wayang kulit puppets, particularly the main characters. Goat hide is too thin and is only suitable for making smaller supporting characters, while buffalo hide is too thick,” he explained.
According to Che Ann, the cowhide, preferably still fresh, must first be dried naturally under the sun until it is completely dry.

“If the weather is really hot, it takes about a month for the hide to dry up completely. Only then is the hair removed manually before an image of the character is sketched onto the surface of the hide,” he said.
Once the sketch is complete, the most demanding stage, requiring precision and patience, begins.

Using nothing more than nails of various sizes and a metal hammer, Che Ann carefully punches thousands of holes in the cured cowhide, creating intricate patterns through precisely placed perforations.
These perforated patterns allow light to pass through, projecting stunning details of the puppet, such as its facial features, garment and accessories, onto the white screen.
The tools used may be simple, but every strike must be carefully executed as even a small mistake can affect the entire carved pattern.
“Modern machines can speed up the punching process, but the aesthetics are not the same. Hand carving has its own value and precision that cannot be replicated by machines,” he said.
Che Ann said the time required to complete a character depends on its level of complexity.

He can complete three simple characters, such as those of ordinary villagers or attendants, in a day. However, main characters such as Seri Rama, or complex elements such as the banyan tree and palace structures, can take up to a week to complete.
“These main characters have many floral carvings and intricate patterns, so they require complete concentration,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Using only nails of various sizes and a metal hammer, Kang Boon Ann—a practitioner of Kelantan *wayang kulit* (shadow puppetry)—punches thousands of tiny holes into the leather surface to create floral motifs, traditional costumes, crowns, and the various accessories that define each character's identity. While the tools used may be simple, every perforation requires meticulous care, as even a minor error could compromise the entire carved design. — Bernama pic
Own identity, philosophy
For Che Ann, preserving the Kelantan wayang kulit art form’s tradition means adhering to the original “rules” established by the earlier generations of tok dalang.

“Every character (portrayed by the puppets) has its own identity and philosophy. We cannot violate these aspects. For example, the puppet portraying Seri Rama must be green in colour, while it is red for his younger brother Laksamana.

“If we simply change the colours, audiences or other practitioners will say that we have strayed from the characters’ original essence,” he said, adding that there are more than 100 characters in the world of wayang kulit.
“This art form is a reflection of human life. There are rulers and ordinary people, the elderly and the young, as well as protagonists and antagonists,” he said.
For puppets portraying secondary characters, however, Che Ann has greater freedom to experiment with colours.
“Even then, we must respect traditional motifs to ensure that the identity of Kelantan wayang kulit remains intact,” he said.
While demand for wayang kulit performances has been slow, the market for the puppets tells a different story.
Through consistent publicity, including live demonstrations of puppet-making on his digital platforms, Che Ann receives a steady stream of orders for his wayang kulit puppets.
The best-sellers are those portraying the Seri Rama, Sita Dewi, Hanuman Kera Putih and Rawana characters.
“Most people buy them for their personal collections or as exclusive decorations for their homes or galleries. They appreciate the artistic value of the carvings on each character,” he said.
Interestingly, orders have not only come from the domestic market but also from Singapore and Switzerland.
The large and intricately structured pieces are sold at about RM600 each, while the prices of others range from RM300 to RM550 apiece.

Although Che Ann is aware that his handcrafted puppets could fetch more than RM1,000 each if sold in places like Central Market in Kuala Lumpur, he prefers to keep his prices affordable so that the heritage art remains accessible to people from all walks of life.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Special pigments are applied to the cowhide surface to bring out the colors of *wayang kulit* (shadow puppet) figures—a process that truly tests precision and patience. — Bernama pic
Raw materials
Despite continued demand for puppets, Che Ann said fulfilling orders has become increasingly challenging due to difficulties in sourcing the main raw material - cowhide.

“Cattle today are mostly fed commercial feed. As a result, their hides are too fatty, less firm and not as bright in colour when dried. The fatty texture also makes it more difficult to punch holes in the hide and affects the even absorption of paint.
“Cows, in the past, grazed naturally on the grass. Their hides were cleaner, brighter and much more suitable for carving,” he said.

Adding to the challenge, hides from local cattle breeds are becoming increasingly difficult to source as the market is now dominated by larger imported breeds such as Charolais, whose hides are excessively thick.
“Local cowhide is now very precious. Sometimes, it takes a month just to obtain a single piece,” he said.
Despite being made without preservatives, wayang kulit puppets can last for decades, provided they are strictly protected from moisture.

“The biggest enemies are moisture and damp spaces. When the monsoon season arrives, all the puppets have to be taken out of storage and aired or dried again to prevent mould, which can damage the hide’s texture,” he said.
For Che Ann, his three decades of dedication to preserving the wayang kulit tradition would be in vain if the skill of carving puppets were to die with him.

Recognising this, he actively conducts puppet-making workshops at schools and universities, as well as at programmes organised by cultural agencies such as the National Department for Culture and Arts.

Thanks to these efforts, more people are beginning to understand that wayang kulit is not merely about puppets moving behind a cloth screen, but a highly skilled heritage craft that demands discipline, patience and painstaking work.
“As we say, you cannot love what you do not know. My task now is to give people the opportunity to ‘know’ the craft by showing them how the puppets are made.
“Once they have tried hammering the nails themselves, they begin to appreciate and love this art form,” he said.
As long as his hands remain strong enough to wield a metal hammer and his eyes sharp enough to guide each strike, Che Ann is determined to keep carving.
Every hole he punches into a piece of cowhide is a small assurance that Kelantan’s wayang kulit heritage will continue to live on for generations to come. — Bernama
8f7b1cb69f1f19c8: Pelancaran 118 pakej dan itinerari berasaskan pengalaman oleh Tourism Malaysia memberi gambaran tentang perubahan yang semakin diperlukan dalam sektor pelancongan negara.
Malaysia tidak lagi boleh bergantung semata-mata kepada pantai yang cantik, pusat beli-belah, hotel atau senarai tempat menarik untuk memikat pelancong.
Persaingan pelancongan semakin sengit. Banyak destinasi lain juga menawarkan kemudahan dan tarikan yang hampir sama.

Justeru, apa yang boleh membezakan Malaysia ialah pengalaman yang sukar ditiru negara lain — makanan, budaya, kehidupan masyarakat setempat, hasil pertanian serta interaksi secara langsung dengan komuniti.
Itulah potensi yang cuba diketengahkan menerusi tiga inisiatif Tourism Malaysia, iaitu Edu+ 2.0, EatVenture dan Taste of Orchard.
Daripada keseluruhan 118 pakej itu, 29 diperkenalkan melalui Edu+ 2.0, 23 menerusi EatVenture dan 66 lagi di bawah Taste of Orchard.

Ketua Pengarah Tourism Malaysia, Mohd Amirul Rizal Abdul Rahim, menyifatkan ketiga-tiga inisiatif itu sebagai produk pasaran khusus yang menyasarkan kumpulan pelancong tertentu, sama ada domestik mahupun antarabangsa.

Pendekatan seperti ini penting menjelang Kempen Melawat Malaysia 2026-2027 kerana pelancong perlu diberikan lebih banyak sebab bukan sahaja untuk datang ke Malaysia, tetapi tinggal lebih lama dan kembali semula.
Bukan sekadar lawatan kampus
Edu+ 2.0, misalnya, membuka peluang menjadikan pendidikan sebahagian daripada pengalaman melancong.
Program jangka pendek bagi pelajar antarabangsa boleh digunakan untuk memperkenalkan budaya dan warisan Malaysia sambil mewujudkan pertukaran budaya yang lebih bermakna.
Namun, pakej pendidikan tidak seharusnya berakhir dengan lawatan ke kampus atau beberapa aktiviti ringkas.

Ia perlu mempunyai hasil pembelajaran yang jelas, kandungan bersesuaian dengan umur peserta, pengurusan keselamatan yang baik serta kerjasama konsisten antara institusi pendidikan, agensi perjalanan dan pengendali destinasi.
Tanpa elemen itu, sukar untuk menjadikan pendidikan sebagai produk pelancongan yang benar-benar mempunyai nilai.
Makanan bukan sekadar untuk dimakan
EatVenture pula memanfaatkan satu daripada kekuatan terbesar Malaysia, iaitu makanan.
Namun, pelancongan gastronomi tidak seharusnya difahami sebagai membawa pelancong dari satu restoran ke restoran lain untuk makan.
Nilainya menjadi lebih tinggi apabila pelancong memahami cerita di sebalik sesuatu hidangan — dari mana bahannya diperoleh, bagaimana ia disediakan dan siapa yang mengekalkan tradisi tersebut.
Lawatan ke pasar, demonstrasi memasak, pertemuan dengan pengusaha tempatan atau peluang menyediakan sendiri hidangan boleh mengubah aktiviti makan menjadi pengalaman budaya.
Inilah jenis pengalaman yang boleh kekal dalam ingatan pelancong selepas mereka pulang.
Dari dusun kepada produk pelancongan
Taste of Orchard pula mempunyai potensi besar untuk memperkukuh agropelancongan.
Durian, harum manis, koko, gula apong, empurau dan nanas bukan sekadar hasil pertanian. Setiap satunya mempunyai identiti yang berkait rapat dengan tempat dan komuniti tertentu.
Jika dibangunkan dengan baik, lawatan ke dusun atau ladang boleh menghasilkan nilai ekonomi lebih besar daripada sekadar penjualan hasil pertanian.
Sebuah farmstay, misalnya, boleh menggabungkan pengalaman mempelajari penternakan ikan tilapia, mengurus kebun durian dan melihat demonstrasi penyediaan makanan tradisional.
Apabila lebih banyak aktiviti tersedia dalam satu kawasan, pelancong mempunyai sebab untuk tinggal lebih lama.
Perbelanjaan mereka pula boleh dinikmati bukan sahaja pemilik lokasi, tetapi pengusaha inap desa, petani, pemandu pelancong, pengusaha makanan dan perniagaan kecil setempat.
Namun, agropelancongan mempunyai cabaran tersendiri.
Musim buah, cuaca, kebersihan, keselamatan pengunjung, kapasiti ladang dan mutu penerangan kepada pelancong perlu diurus secara konsisten.
118 pakej belum tentu 118 produk berjaya
Dalam keterujaan memperkenalkan 118 pakej, satu perkara perlu diingat: kewujudan sesuatu produk tidak bermakna ia secara automatik akan mendapat permintaan.
Dalam industri pelancongan, mempunyai produk dan mempunyai produk yang boleh dijual adalah dua perkara berbeza.
Pakej yang baik perlu mudah ditemui, mudah difahami, mudah ditempah dan mudah dibayar.
Jika produk hanya menarik dalam bahan promosi tetapi pelancong sukar mendapatkan harga, jadual, kaedah pengangkutan atau saluran tempahan, potensi itu tidak akan bertukar menjadi jualan sebenar.
Setiap pakej perlu mempunyai maklumat jelas mengenai harga, tempoh program, kesesuaian peserta, bahasa digunakan, akses pengangkutan serta kaedah tempahan.
Kandungan digital juga perlu menunjukkan pengalaman sebenar yang bakal diperoleh pelancong, bukan sekadar gambar lokasi yang cantik.
Pelancong hari ini membuat keputusan dengan pantas berdasarkan video, ulasan pengguna dan kemudahan membuat tempahan.
Produk yang menarik tetapi rumit untuk dibeli boleh kehilangan pelanggan kepada pilihan lain yang lebih mudah.
Jangan korbankan keaslian
Kualiti turut perlu diberi perhatian, khususnya apabila pakej melibatkan komuniti tempatan.
Pelancongan berasaskan pengalaman sering dijual atas nama keaslian, tetapi keaslian tidak boleh dijadikan alasan untuk mengabaikan standard perkhidmatan.
Pengusaha tempatan memerlukan latihan dalam layanan pelanggan, penceritaan, keselamatan dan pengurusan aduan.
Pada masa sama, pengalaman yang ditawarkan juga tidak harus terlalu diseragamkan sehingga menghilangkan identiti tempatan yang menjadi sebab pelancong mahu datang.
Keseimbangan antara kualiti dan keaslian inilah yang perlu dijaga.
Ukur tempahan, bukan jumlah pakej
Menjelang Kempen Melawat Malaysia 2026-2027, kejayaan inisiatif seperti ini tidak seharusnya diukur berdasarkan jumlah pakej yang dilancarkan semata-mata.

Ukuran lebih bermakna ialah berapa banyak tempahan yang diterima, berapa lama pelancong tinggal, berapa banyak mereka berbelanja, sama ada mereka datang semula dan sejauh mana wang dibelanjakan kekal dalam komuniti tempatan.
Kita juga perlu melihat sama ada pakej berkenaan berjaya membawa pelancong keluar daripada destinasi tradisional dan menyebarkan manfaat ekonomi ke kawasan lain.
Pelancaran Edu+ 2.0, EatVenture dan Taste of Orchard adalah langkah ke arah yang betul kerana ia mengubah tumpuan daripada sekadar menjual destinasi kepada menjual pengalaman.
Malaysia sememangnya mempunyai makanan, budaya, pertanian dan komuniti yang mempunyai identiti tersendiri.
Cabaran sebenar sekarang ialah mengubah kekayaan itu menjadi pengalaman yang sanggup dibayar pelancong dan pada masa sama memberi pulangan adil kepada komuniti.
Jika itu dapat dilakukan secara konsisten, Kempen Melawat Malaysia 2026-2027 bukan sahaja boleh membawa lebih ramai pelawat.

Ia boleh mengubah cara Malaysia menjual dirinya kepada dunia — daripada sekadar menawarkan tempat untuk dilihat kepada mencipta pengalaman yang membuatkan pelancong mahu tinggal lebih lama, berbelanja lebih banyak dan datang semula.
Penulis ialah pensyarah Fakulti Pengurusan Hotel dan Pelancongan Universiti Teknologi Mara.

fd382010ba317855: In 1947, a young Malay woman entered medical school in Singapore; she was the only Malay woman in her intake. I wonder what it felt like to walk into that classroom each morning, knowing there was nobody quite like you there.

Dr Hasmah Ali, also known as Siti Hasmah, went on to graduate, practise medicine and lead public health services. With her passing at the age of 100, we have lost someone who helped change what a doctor could look like in Malaysia.

Many knew her as the wife of a prime minister. She was that, and carried the role for decades, but she was a doctor before she was a public figure, and her medical work deserves to be remembered on its own terms.

After graduating in 1955, she worked in a hospital before devoting herself to maternal and child health in Kedah. In 1965, she became the first woman to be appointed as a medical officer in the maternal and child health department; in 1974, she became the state’s first female maternal and child health officer. She also led the rural health training school in Jitra.
Those appointments gave her responsibility for people’s care and for the health workers who would provide it.
Her teams travelled to villages to provide immunisation and health education. They worked with traditional midwives and spoke with families about pregnancy, childbirth and caring for newborns.

Hasmah understood that a mother could not always arrange transport, leave her responsibilities and appear at a clinic simply because a doctor wanted her there. Healthcare had to make the journey towards her.

I find that part of her story especially moving. It is easy to praise a pioneer for being a trailblazer. It takes longer to understand the patient work that followed: returning to communities, earning trust and teaching others to care for mothers and children.
She helped build a health service in which a woman’s judgment could guide that work.

The norm she challenged has changed profoundly for Malaysian women who came after her such as Dr Narimah Awin, who went on to lead family health services and advise the World Health Organization on maternal and reproductive health; Dr Adeeba Kamarulzaman, whose work on HIV took her into global leadership; and Dr Jemilah Mahmood, who founded Mercy Malaysia and now leads work in planetary health.

And of course, Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, who took her experience as a doctor into national political life while continuing to support programmes and changes within the health landscape. Most recently, Dr BP Nirmala, a Malaysian cancer epidemiologist, joined the World Health Organization (WHO) science council this year.

For me, this is also personal. Dr S Saunthari leads the National Cancer Society of Malaysia, of which I now serve as a director. She is also the first Malaysian president-elect of the global NCD Alliance.

Around these well-known names are many more women leading wards, district services, classrooms and research teams. Each has earned their place. Together, they show how far women’s authority in medicine now reaches.
Hasmah lived another side of medicine when she was treated for breast cancer. In 2019, she spoke publicly about that experience.

The doctor who had spent years urging women to care for their health let us hear from her as a patient. Her illness did not define her life, but her willingness to speak about it was another way of making women’s health visible.

We should be careful not to assume that there is a straight line from one woman to the next. Hasmah did not create every opportunity that followed, and the women who came after her built their own careers.

But the legacy of her achievement was to help change expectations of them. She showed Malaysians a Malay woman practising medicine, teaching health workers and leading a service at a time when that was a rare sight.

She remains an icon because her example still asks something of us. When a young woman finds herself the only one in the room, will we recognise her ability and make room for her to lead? When a patient cannot reach care, will we go closer to them?
Hasmah answered those questions with her life. Her light continues in the women who enter medicine, in those who lead it, and in the people whose lives they change.

And as much as we will remember the former prime minister’s wife, we will also remember the doctor who went to mothers in the villages of Kedah, the teacher who prepared others to care for them, and the woman who spoke openly when she herself faced cancer.
Hasmah was always her own woman. Her work lives on in the people it reached; her example lives on in the women who follow. And she will remain, very dearly, in our hearts.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect the views of FMT.
93fd3639b1f83bb0: PETALING JAYA: Malaysia is home to some of the world’s most beautiful coastlines. But each year, an estimated 73,098 metric tonnes of plastic waste from the country makes its way into the sea. That makes Malaysia the world’s third-largest contributor of ocean plastic by total mass.
But not everyone is willing to turn a blind eye.
“MY Clean Beach” is a Malaysian environmental advocacy movement co-founded in 2019 by Geeva Samynathan who grew up near the golden sands of Teluk Cempedak in Kuantan.
“We started ‘MY Clean Beach’ over eight years ago, and it’s truly a passion initiative. We didn’t really see it growing at this scale when we started,” she told FMT Lifestyle.
“One day we were walking at a beach in Perak, and it really hurt us almost instantly to see the kind of trash on the ground. That’s how it all started.”
What began with a couple of friends organising beach clean-ups grew into an internationally recognised initiative, removing nearly 30,000kg of waste over the years.
Today, the team relies on a growing network of community volunteers from all walks of life, who give up their Saturdays to get their hands dirty.
“We are a group of people who just truly love nature. Everyone on the team has the same agenda - to make a little difference,” said Geeva, a certified sustainability (ESG) practitioner.

Today, the organisation mainly works with corporate clients on two- to three-hour CSR clean-ups at locations across Malaysia. One of their biggest clean-up efforts saw the team collect 1,200kg of trash in a single session.
“We focus on corporate events because we realise working adults have a voice, and they can share what they learn with their families and communities,” Geeva said.
FMT Lifestyle joined the MY Clean Beach team for a morning beach clean-up in Sepang in mid-September.
Once the waste is brought back to the base, it is sorted into different categories, including glass, tin and metal, general waste, plastic, and more.
“We collect data, which is published openly. We even go to the extent of counting how many cigarette butts and straws were collected.”
Geeva said single-use plastics such as straws, bottles and food packaging make up most of their hauls, followed by cigarette butts, while diapers also occasionally turn up.
Fishing nets and broken glass are also often collected, posing safety risks to both people and wildlife.
The team follows a strict zero-waste framework, meaning 100% of the collected waste is diverted from landfills and repurposed.
Their zero-waste philosophy doesn’t stop at the trash they collect; it starts with what they bring to the beach.

The team avoids standard black plastic rubbish bags, and instead provides certified compostable bags for its clean-ups. They also avoid using single-use latex and nitrile gloves for both environmental and practical reasons, as these can tear easily during clean-ups. Instead, volunteers are provided with heavy-duty, washable fabric and rubber-coated work gloves.
The group also organises tree-planting initiatives and educational programmes aimed at promoting better waste management.

While Geeva has no plans to slow down, she hopes more Malaysians will step up and lend a hand. She said that although awareness has grown and more volunteers have come forward in recent years, beach clean-ups alone will not solve the problem.

“We clean the beach today and the ocean still washes up more trash the next day. Malaysians love to go for picnics, but they can tell you, ‘I forgot to bring a plastic bag to wrap up the trash’. In terms of behaviour shift, I think we’re still very far away.”
Eight years and tonnes of trash later, there’s still plenty of work to do. Hopefully, one day, there’ll be less rubbish waiting for them.

JOHOR BARU: Malaysia and Singapore tested their joint response to cross-border incidents involving the Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link yesterday, ahead of its launch on Jan 1.

The testing, dubbed Table Top Exercise, focused on strengthening coordination between the authorities and government agencies of both countries in managing emergencies that could disrupt the link's operations.

Organised by the National Security Council in collaboration with Singapore's Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), the exercise also tested and validated seven jointly developed standard operating procedures (SOPs).
The framework sets out who takes charge when an incident occurs during a journey in either country's territory and at the 17-metre border stretch.
It also sets out the guidelines in providing mutual assistance and controlled cross-border deployment of emergency personnel.
Johor police chief Datuk Ab Rahaman Arsad attended the closing ceremony.
The drill also reflected the security agencies' efforts to ensure that incident procedures are clearly established and effectively activated.
The RTS Link, connecting Bukit Chagar in Johor Baru and Woodlands North in Singapore, is expected to significantly increase cross-border connectivity.
25b648a375be821d: WASHINGTON: The US justice department asked a court Wednesday to punish federal judges in Minnesota who spoke to the media and criticised aggressive raids carried out in that state by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
It was the latest twist in a clash between the Trump administration and federal judges who have at times thwarted his drive to deport millions of immigrants lacking residency papers.

On Sept 17, The New York Times published an article that quoted Judge Patrick Schiltz, the chief judge at Minnesota's federal district court during a series of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids last winter in Minneapolis, and six of the judge's colleagues on the bench.

Schiltz had already gained notoriety during the peak of those raids by saying publicly that ICE had probably violated more court orders in January 2026 than other federal agencies had in their entire decades of existence.

In an interview for the Times article, Schiltz said ICE's behaviour had sparked such chaos in his court that it "created a grave threat to the rule of law." He said he thought the violations of court orders stemmed mainly from incompetence and staffing shortages.
It is rare for a judge to speak out publicly like that, the Times said.

He and the other six judges quoted in the article declined to talk about ongoing cases, but they did agree to address the tumult of last winter during the ICE operation dubbed "Metro Surge" and the tension it triggered between Schiltz's court and the justice department, the paper said.

The justice department announced Wednesday it had filed a judicial misconduct complaint against Schiltz and the other six judges at a federal appeals court. It accuses them of ethics violations by speaking publicly about cases pending in court.
The department asked an appeals court to investigate these judges, Attorney General Todd Blanche told a press conference.

The department has "asked that these judges recuse themselves from every case involving DHS, either criminal or civil in nature, because of the obvious bias they have shown in this article with the New York Times," Blanche said. DHS stands for Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE.

During operation "Metro Surge" ICE agents shot and killed two American citizens taking part in street protests against the immigration raids, triggering national outrage and prompting the administration to wind down the operation.
The administration says the raids netted the arrest of 4,000 people who were in the country illegally.
5bce7b66b3872438: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump announced Wednesday US$200 billion in US energy investments from South Korea, including US$54 billion toward a long-discussed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska.

Besides the Alaska LNG project and pipeline, the Trump administration announced eight new nuclear plants and a large natural gas-fired plant in Texas that would be supported by the government of South Korea, Trump said.
The announcement details South Korea's previous pledges to make good on a tariff deal with Trump.

South Korea had agreed to invest US$350 billion in the United States and boost its purchases of American energy as part of a July 2025 trade deal with Trump that set 15 per cent tariffs on South Korean goods imported into the United States.

Top Trump administration officials, including Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, joined the president for an Oval Office ceremony with Alaska Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is facing a tough reelection contest in November.

The Alaska project, championed by Glenfarne Group, a New York- and Houston-based industrial project developer, envisions the construction of an 800-mile pipeline to transport natural gas from the Alaska North Slope to a liquefaction facility near Anchorage to prepare for export to Asia.
Alaska officials have considered such a project in the past, but have not moved ahead due to questions about project costs and consumer demand for the LNG.
While Alaska has decades of history as a petroleum producer, environmental concerns have historically constrained some developments.

But the Trump administration has largely brushed aside environmental concerns, canceling regulations to reduce emissions that cause global warming while pursuing an "energy dominance" agenda that favours fossil fuel development.
The industrial ramp-up envisioned for the energy projects also faces a potential labor shortfall.

The United States needs to fill an estimated 1.7 million skilled trade openings through 2035, according to a report released Wednesday by the Alliance for America's Skilled Trades, an organisation of Ford, Blackstone, Nvidia and other large companies.
The report found today's training programme produce just 55 workers for every 100 needed.--AFP
deed1b087192eaa4: ROME: Italy defender Giorgio Scalvini said Wednesday the Azzurri were still defining themselves under new coach Roberto Mancini as they prepare to take on Zinedine Zidane's France in the Nations League this week.

JOHOR is intensifying efforts to protect the critically endangered Malayan tiger, with the Endau-Rompin National Park identified as a key habitat.

State Health and Environment Committee chairman Ling Tian Soon said Johor was working with the federal government to improve the prey base, expand camera traps, as well as intensify patrols and enforcement.

He said the measures were discussed during the National Tiger Implementation Working Group (MyTWG) meeting with the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry in Putrajaya on Tuesday.
"Based on the 2020 survey data, the number of Malayan tigers in the wild was estimated at no more than 150.

His comments followed the ministry's report that the Malayan tiger population has shown signs of improvement, though the latest figure has yet to be revealed.
The First National Tiger Survey (2016–2020) found fewer than 150 Malayan tigers in the wild.
The protected species is found only in Peninsular Malaysia and is classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
The Endau-Rompin National Park is one of the country's three main tiger landscapes, featuring an isolated but increasing subpopulation, according to the IUCN.
Ling said the Malayan tiger was more than a national wildlife treasure for Johor.
"We will continue to support and cooperate in efforts to conserve the Malayan tiger.

b6c001c7464439bc: LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday said there were "strong indications" Iran was involved in suspicious activity at a UK airbase that triggered a major security incident this weekend.

A local resident who rang the police said she saw a group of masked men near the vans, which were blocking a road in a village next to the military base.
The case was plunged into confusion when UK police released on bail five British men it had arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.
After three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said Tuesday they had found no explosives in the vehicles, but they had retrieved a "quantity of petrol."
Then on Wednesday, The Times newspaper reported that the incident had been foiled after one of the five suspects tipped off the police before the group was apprehended.

ac6baad9d96fd47b: KUALA LUMPUR: There is a Scrabble board on the table at Merdeka Grill, the letters arranged across it to spell three words that have survived 71 years: I LOVE YOU.
Dr Mahathir Mohamad is leaning over the table, looking at the tiles. Around him are dinner, pastries, city lights and family.
It is a recreation, but not just any family game.
The scene has been staged by his grandchildren to recreate something their grandfather did for their grandmother, Dr Hasmah Mohamad Ali, in 1955.
The original was much simpler.
According to their son Mokhzani Mahathir, April 23 is the date his parents regard as the beginning of their love.
It means so much to them that they have continued to celebrate it over the years, sometimes giving it more significance than their wedding anniversary.
There was just one problem in 1955.
Mahathir was too shy to say the words. So he spelt them.
That detail, shared by Mokhzani after Hasmah’s death at 100, adds a wonderfully intimate scene to a love story Malaysians have heard in many versions over the years.
The young medical student who would one day speak before parliaments and presidents apparently could not bring himself to tell the woman he loved what he was feeling.
Scrabble gave him another way.
He arranged the letters and let the board do the talking.
It sounds almost impossibly old-fashioned now, which is perhaps what makes it so charming.
Seven decades later, Mokhzani’s children decided to recreate the moment for their grandparents at Merdeka Grill at Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur inside the Merdeka 118 tower.
The photographs capture Mahathir at the table, his hands close to the tiles, while another brings the message into full view: I LOVE YOU.
The setting is more elaborate than the original, but Mokhzani says the essential detail remained unchanged.
His father was still too shy to say it aloud.
“Maybe because we were there,” he said.
“Old school.”
It is an extraordinary little detail to emerge after Hasmah’s passing because it gives a private face to a relationship whose public story has been told many times.

They met in 1947 as medical students at King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore. Mahathir remembered competing with five other young men to help carry Hasmah’s books. When she later struggled with a paper, he offered her free tuition.
He eventually told her he loved her, too. Hasmah would recall decades later that this was the most romantic thing he had ever done.
They married in 1956 and spent the next 70 years building a family, pursuing medical careers and navigating the demands of public life.
They argued, too. Hasmah once recalled that after a quarrel they would simply go out for a meal.
Mahathir later described tolerance as essential to a lasting marriage: accepting that the person you love is not necessarily going to change.
Perhaps the Scrabble story explains something else about them.
For all the years they spent in public view, some of the most meaningful moments belonged only to the two of them.
April 23 was one of those moments.

94cc12d897af68ec: GENEVA: The Swiss Football Association (SFV) announced Wednesday it was withdrawing its support for beleaguered incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

Several leading European national associations have pulled their support for Infantino, after he caused uproar in July with proposals to create a commercial subsidiary to run Fifa's biggest events, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.
The SFV's decision carries weight as Infantino is Swiss, and both Fifa and European football's governing body Uefa are based in Switzerland.
The SFV said its executive board met on Friday and "decided to withdraw the support it had declared in June 2026 for Gianni Infantino's candidacy for a further term as Fifa president".

Infantino's plan would have allowed private investors to acquire stakes in a company created under the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) initiative. The backlash that followed led to the proposals being quickly shelved.
The SFV said events in recent months raised fundamental questions over leadership, governance, transparency and decision-making processes with world football's governing body.

It cited Infantino's FFE plans and the lifting of red-carded United States forward Folarin Balogun's one-match suspension during this year's World Cup, following a phone call to Infantino from US President Donald Trump.
SFV president Peter Knabel said that Swiss football's governing body expected Fifa's leadership to uphold the highest standards of transparency, accountability and institutional responsibility.
He said Infantino's proposals last week for "a consultation" with national federations to reform Fifa's governance sent an important signal, and could contribute to improving the situation.
However, "key questions regarding the background, responsibilities and decision-making processes remain unanswered", said Knabel.
"As these have not been convincingly clarified, we cannot justify continuing to support Gianni Infantino's candidacy."

Uefa -- the regional federation that represents World Cup holders Spain and football powerhouses such as France, England and Germany -- is leading the opposition to Infantino, calling openly for his removal.
The SFV, a Uefa member, insisted its decision did not signal a move away from constructive cooperation within Fifa and the global football community.

As the association for the country where Fifa and Uefa are based, "the SFV is aware of its special responsibility and will continue to champion transparency, credible and reliable structure, rules-based decision-making processes", it said.
It called for a strong and united global football community characterised by integrity.
Infantino retains the support of 2034 World Cup hosts Saudi Arabia, while African football's governing body CAF and South America's Conmebol are also supportive.
Candidate nominations for next March's Fifa election must be submitted by November 18. Infantino is the only candidate so far.
b0303a3923afae1d: MILWAUKEE: The United States is pushing for action against excess industrial capacity that drives prices down unfairly, Washington's top trade envoy said Wednesday on the sidelines of a G20 meeting, with some countries – excluding China – agreeing to a plan that includes reducing subsidies.

The developments came as officials from the Group of 20 major economies convened in the Midwestern city of Milwaukee over two days, with a group of countries separately agreeing on a framework to counter "persistent" excess steel production.
Overcapacity is a criticism often leveled against China, with accusations that it produces more than it consumes, flooding markets. Beijing rejects these claims.
"We're releasing a Milwaukee framework to take coordinated action on steel excess capacity," top US trade official Jamieson Greer told reporters Wednesday.

"Every country will do what they think is appropriate. We want to coordinate those measures," Greer added. "The United States has taken robust measures, and it probably makes sense for other countries to do that too."
He did not elaborate on whether he meant for countries to raise trade barriers on Chinese steel.
The framework was released after a meeting of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity. Its 28 members include the European Union, Australia, Japan and South Korea – but not China.
Asked about his message to partners this week on overcapacity, China's international trade representative Li Chenggang told AFP early Wednesday that G20 members had yet to discuss the topic.

Besides plans to reduce or eliminate "market-distorting subsidies," members of the steel global forum also agreed to boost data sharing to help identify "suspicious patterns of steel trade," according to the framework.
It added that, if needed, members would also take "trade measures" against countries that overproduce. Such measures could include tariffs.
- FEW BREAKTHROUGHS -
As G20 trade ministers opened talks Wednesday, a traditional "family photo" was taken twice, allowing European leaders to be separated from Russia's representative, sources told AFP.
European leaders have declined to appear with Russia in G20 photos, with some noting this year that doing so sends a troubling message following Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump's global tariffs also cast a pall over the G20 talks, pushing countries to seek cooperation outside the world's biggest economy.
The meetings come amid a deepening US-Canada trade war, waves of US tariffs and Trump's investigations into member countries over excess industrial capacity.
Analysts expect few breakthroughs as trade tensions simmer.
Countries are seeking deals with the Trump administration, with India pushing to get a trade pact over the finish line. Brazil said it held a "constructive" in-person meeting with Greer too.
Still, the threat of further tariffs looms even over those that have struck deals, as US investigations into overcapacity target 16 trading partners including China, the EU, Japan and India.
Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski urged Wednesday for a lowering of trade barriers.

"I do hope that our US partners will stick to all settlements that were made," he added, referring to an earlier deal between the United States and the European Union to cap Trump's duties on the bloc at 15 per cent.
Of such tariff deals, Greer told reporters Tuesday: "We will certainly take them into account."
But he added that he was not in a rush to reach a pact with Canada, where certain products now face a US ban due to their trade spat.
"Eventually, it will happen," he said.
Also on the agenda this week are efforts to eliminate forced labour and the targeting of food access to pressure others.
Domanski condemned "all actions taken by Russia against the export of agriculture products from Ukraine" in their war.
Poland is not a permanent G20 member but has been invited to the table this year as Washington holds the grouping's rotating presidency. In turn, US officials have excluded South Africa.
The G20 trade ministerial comes after finance ministers met in Asheville, setting the stage for a leaders' summit in Miami.
The G20 comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union.--AFP

98405d2366246f93: NEW YORK: Nasdaq climbed on Wednesday and the S&P 500 dipped, but both indexes notched their second straight quarterly gains, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading cooled expectations that Federal Reserve policymakers would hike rates in October.
The US commerce department reported the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE) increased 3.4% on an annual basis in August, below the 3.7% estimate of economists polled by Reuters.

Separately, the final reading of second-quarter GDP data was revised higher to a 2.2% annualised rate, thanks to solid consumer spending and investments helping to fuel the buildout of AI infrastructure.

The rising prices of crude oil from the US-Iran war and sky-high diesel fuel costs have stoked inflation worries and pushed US Treasury yields higher. Fed officials have indicated more rate hikes might be needed if price pressures fail to moderate after the central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points this month.

Stocks lost ground heading into the closing bell, however, as the 2-year US Treasury note yield, which typically moves in step with Fed interest-rate expectations, turned slightly higher on the day. Longer-dated yields kept climbing on expectations for solid economic growth.

Market expectations for a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed's October meeting slumped to about 37%, according to CME's FedWatch Tool, from roughly 51% in the prior session and nearly 71% a week ago.
Analysts also noted that recent methodology changes in calculating PCE by the Bureau of Economic Analysis contributed to a lower reading.

"What the market is focused on is, is the economy continuing to grow and can it manage those higher interest rates? And I would say so far, the market has looked kind of like history that when the economy is growing, when profits are strong, when there's a secular theme, it will look past higher interest rates," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial in Troy, Michigan.

"However... if these higher rates stay at these elevated levels for longer, it's likely to start doing potentially more damage to the bond side of the portfolio, it could limit credit or available credit. And if investors start to feel those conditions could weigh on economic growth or weigh on corporate profitability over the next quarter or two, then I think you would see a very swift negative reaction in the market."
S&P, Nasdaq notch quarterly gains

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 443.87 points, or 0.86%, to 50,906.05, the S&P 500 lost 19.30 points, or 0.25%, to 7,651.54 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 63.52 points, or 0.24%, to 26,861.06. The S&P had risen as much as 0.7% while the Nasdaq had climbed as much as 1.2% on the session.

For the month, the S&P 500 fell 0.45%, the Nasdaq rose 1.86%, and the Dow fell 4.29%. The Dow snapped a five-month streak of gains while the S&P fell for the third month in four. The Nasdaq gained for a second straight month.
Both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq recorded their second straight quarterly advances and fifth in the past six. The Dow saw a quarterly decline for the second time in three.

Most megacap and growth stocks ticked higher, with Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia each rising ato lifting the S&P 500 tech index 0.6% as the best-performing sector on the day. However, nine of the 11 major S&P sectors ended the day lower.
Private payrolls rise in September

A reading on the labour market showed private employment rose by 90,000 jobs this month after a downwardly revised 36,000 in August, the ADP National Employment Report showed. The data was the latest in a string of reports on the job market this week that will culminate in Friday's key government payrolls report.

Without addressing the softer-than-expected inflation data, Fed Governor Lisa Cook said she is committed to bringing inflation down without harming the labour market as price pressures have been too high for too long.

Among other movers, Hewlett Packard Enterprise climbed 3.9% after the AI server maker raised its long-term revenue growth forecast for its networking business and announced a US$1.2 billion deal with Vultr.
Moderna slumped 5.3% after brokerage Citigroup downgraded its rating on the biotech company to "sell" from "neutral."
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.66-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.51-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.
The S&P 500 posted 11 new 52-week highs and 24 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 54 new highs and 212 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 18.13 billion shares, compared with the 17.06 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.
6b2bc4023a766cb3: COPENHAGEN: Portugal captain Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Wednesday that he had left the team's training camp in Denmark after coach Jorge Jesus told reporters that the striker would be dropped for their next match.
Ronaldo had been due to train with his team-mates at the Parken stadium in Copenhagen on Wednesday but left abruptly after Jesus's press conference.

"There was no incident whatsoever," Jesus told reporters.

2ef764de3e420a81: About 66 million years ago, the Chicxulub asteroid smashed into Earth, kicking up tsunamis and dropping hot debris that annihilated non-avian dinosaurs and many other species. But not everything it left in its wake was destructive. This space rock hit what is now the partially submerged Yucatan Peninsula, and at the bottom of the ocean, the impact generated enough heat to create a hydrothermal system that persisted for 8 million years and may have been a hotbed of life.

When researchers drilled for samples in the impact zone in 2016, they studied the types of rock that had formed as a result of the asteroid strike. This gave more insight into what happened in the immediate and long-term aftermath of this cataclysmic event.

The collision was intense enough to cause deformation far beneath the surface. Subterranean effects reached 35 km (almost 22 miles) down, and included the melting an immense amount of rock. Exposure to seawater made that rock porous. As hot water seeped into the pores, a hydrothermal system formed. The hot water gushing into an isolated region of the freezing depths could have attracted microorganisms and possibly other life forms that were otherwise struggling to survive.

4530dbe65ddfbc46: Mechanical calculators are precise, fascinating gadgets that you wouldn’t think would take well to being 3D printed, but a YouTuber has proved that a pocket-sized unit can be made purely from plastic filament. YouTuber 3D all Workshop detailed his working, but limited, build in a recent video. If you’re familiar with the holy grail of palm-sized mechanical calculators, the Curta, also known as the “pepper mill,” you already have a working understanding of how this 3D-printed calculator works. As detailed in the video, Workshop’s 3D-printed mechanical calculator, like the Curta, relies on a more than 200-year-old component known as the Leibniz stepped drum, named for its inventor, German philosopher and mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. The core concept of the calculator’s central mechanism, like that of many other mechanical calculators, is the Leibniz drum’s teeth of different lengths. There are nine teeth per drum, representing values one through nine, while a zero setting engages none of them. Workshop’s 3D printed calculator can take inputs from 1 to 999, with one drum per digit. You use a lever to move a gear up the drum so that it only activates as many teeth as are needed for a particular number. The same concept is used to input values into the Curta, just in a much more precise manner - one of the big benefits of using machined aluminum over 3D printing filament. As a result of wanting to keep the 3D printed calc’s build palm-sized, the YouTuber was forced to restrict what it’s able to do. It can do addition, and the addition of a multi-wheel enables it to also do multiplication by simply performing multiple sequences of adding the same number. The Curta does multiplication in a similar manner, requiring a user to input their base number and the number of times they want to multiply by addition. Unlike the Curta, Workshop’s calculator can’t subtract, nor can it divide - as its creator explains, there simply wasn’t the room to get all those fiddly bits into a palm-sized device. It’s not clear how large it would have to be to add those functions, but if the 3x-sized 3D printed Curta is any indication - its creator said the increased size was necessary - it’d probably be quite large. Scaling down to Workshop’s tiny 3D printed calculator means plenty of issues were bound to arise, and they definitely did. “There were a lot of problems,” he noted, explaining that “even the tiniest inconsistencies when printing can cause problems.” If you’ve ever used a 3D filament printer, you know how often such inconsistencies pop up. Gears kept binding because of tight 3D-printing tolerances, while backlash (the play between mating mechanical parts) could throw the drums out of sync. Pieces kept breaking during redesigns, and even the vibrations from picking up and using the calculator were enough to disrupt its components. The YouTuber went through roughly 100 design iterations over the two-month project, finally addressing the problems with custom-designed 3D-printed springs and a ratchet mechanism that kept backlash from throwing the drums out of sync. All said, the final build ended up with 109 separate pieces, took 17 print-hours to complete, and used 90g of filament. Despite multiple calls on YouTube for 3D all Workshop to publish, or even sell, his design, he has yet to make it available, so no struggling through a day-long print job for a potentially brief moment playing with this one. In the meantime, you could 3D print the giant Curta, or if you have a couple grand lying around begging to be spent, try to get your hands on an original. ®

3e98ea49575d5b71: The Trump administration's export control policies governing the sale of AI accelerators to China haven't stopped homegrown Huawei from filling the void. In a Q&A-style release this week, the company's rotating chairman Eric Xu claimed that its Ascend line of neural processing units (NPUs) had exceeded Nvidia in Chinese market share. "It's pretty hard to collect data about the market share of Nvidia in China, but based on the data we have collected, Ascend has surpassed Nvidia," he said. "Chinese people have a keen sense of urgency, and will not accept a future in which others decide whether or not we can have access to certain products." Since taking office, the Trump administration has done an about-face on export controls. After imposing new licensing requirements on Nvidia's and AMD's China-spec accelerators in April 2025, the US Commerce Department reversed course that summer, later reaching an arrangement to cut the US government in on a percentage of certain China-bound chip sales. By late last year, the Trump administration loosened restrictions further, announcing that Nvidia would be allowed to sell its more potent H200-series parts to approved Chinese customers for the first time ever. However, the damage was already done. While Uncle Sam had given Jensen Huang its blessing to resume sales, the initial blockade of H20s earlier in the year had set off alarm bells in Beijing. Government officials there began pressuring bit barn operators to transition away from foreign accelerators in favor of homegrown alternatives. During Nvidia's Q2 earnings call, executives revealed that while the company had begun shipments of a small volume of H200 accelerators to the region, they amounted to less than 1 percent of its datacenter revenues. "Even though our chips may be less advanced, at least their supply is assured, so that you don't have to worry about chip supply day in and day out," Xu said. "For the Chinese government, for the domestic industry, and for Huawei, the path forward is undoubtedly to push for full self-sufficiency in terms of chips and the entire semiconductor value chain." As we recently discussed, while Huawei's latest accelerators still fall short of Nvidia's or AMD's on paper, they make up for that deficit with scale. Huawei is currently deploying a 256,000-card Atlas 950 SuperCluster, while its newer architecture is designed to support training and inference for multi-trillion-parameter models and scale to as many as one million NPUs. However, as Xu notes, Huawei likely won't be a threat to Nvidia outside of China for a while. "We don't have enough capacity to satisfy the demand in China. We don't have plans to expand the international market in a fully-fledged way," he said, downplaying reports that Huawei had begun supplying friendly nations with its chips. "The balance between satisfying the needs of domestic customers and those of international customers is actually quite easy," he said when asked about the use of Ascend accelerators to power Malaysia's sovereign AI initiative. "We prioritize Chinese customers who are in urgent demand for compute; outside of China we only supply a very limited number of customers who either have no access to alternative solutions or want an alternative solution." Along with pressure from government officials to transition away from foreign chips, changing software paradigms are making the transition easier for model devs, like DeepSeek, which has been working with Huawei's chips for well over a year now. "The first barrier encountered by Ascend is actually not hardware itself," said Liao Heng, chief scientist of Huawei's HiSilicon. "It's primarily the ecosystem barrier, because two years ago there was still a tremendous software barrier for Ascend." Liao is referring to what's often called the CUDA moat, a software hurdle not unique to China but faced by essentially every competing chipmaker. "There have been drastic changes over the past 18 months," Liao said. He explained that, two years ago, AI training was dominated by PyTorch running atop CUDA, but changes in model architectures have pushed model devs to "mega-kernel-style programming." "CUDA was no longer deemed important by the frontier labs, nowhere near as much as two years ago," he said. To this end, DeepSeek reportedly released several software tools this week aimed at making Huawei’s Ascend accelerators more accessible to other AI labs. ®
